Our contribution is design knowledge grounded in mechanisms for autonomy-supportive digital health decision support systems, comprising concise design principles that can guide SAR-enabled, context-aware assistance toward safety without surveillance and help without dependency, thereby providing a practical path to extend independent living.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114653.a: Integrating machine learning (ML) into decision support systems (DSS) has improved the efficiency and quality of decision making. Yet historical data can embed hidden biases that may lead to unfair outcomes, making algorithmic bias an important societal concern. To address this issue, we develop a fairness-aware DSS based on adversarial learning (AL). The system uses a dual-network architecture: a prediction network that learns task-relevant representations and predicts target outcomes, and an adversarial network that infers protected attributes and thereby helps mitigate bias. As a computationally oriented design science artifact, our DSS embeds fairness norms as executable mechanisms within the model training phase, supporting fairer decisions in practice. We evaluate the model on a Chinese P2P lending dataset and the German Credit dataset. The results show that the proposed approach performs well with respect to four standard fairness criteria, namely unawareness, independence, sufficiency, and separation, while achieving higher predictive accuracy than widely used ML and AL baselines. Overall, this study advances the design of fairness-aware DSS and provides evidence that adversarial learning can reduce algorithmic bias and support fairer decision making.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114654.a: The global scarcity of healthcare professionals poses a significant challenge, impacting the health and well-being of individuals worldwide. Conversational agents offer a novel approach to complement and integrate into existing healthcare systems, potentially enhancing the breadth of healthcare services and optimizing physicians' time utilization. Despite their growing adoption, limited research has examined how communication accommodation strategies used by healthcare conversational agents (HCAs) shape user perceptions and satisfaction. To address this gap, we conducted two laboratory experiments using customized HCAs to investigate the effects of two communication strategies: convergence and naturalness. The findings reveal that both strategies enhance user satisfaction by increasing perceived social presence and empathy. Furthermore, these effects are moderated by users' ideological views on AI (i.e., optimistic or pessimistic attitudes). These insights advance theoretical understanding of communication processes in human–AI interactions and offer practical guidance for improving HCAs in digital healthcare environments.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114655.a: While large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized writing assistance, their widespread misuse poses significant threats to scholarly integrity and authorship originality. Existing detection methods, often relying on single-dimensional features and document-level binary classification, lack the granularity to identify localized LLM involvement and are vulnerable to sophisticated evasion tactics like paraphrasing. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Multi-level Fine-grained Detection (MFD) framework, which integrates low-level statistical, high-level semantic, and deep-level linguistic features to accurately localize LLM-generated content at the sentence level. Specifically, we employ a robustness-aware contrastive learning mechanism trained on adversarially rewritten texts to capture invariant high-level semantic features. Furthermore, we leverage an advanced LLM to extract deep linguistic nuances and contextual patterns that traditional methods overlook. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that MFD outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving an MAE of 0.1347 and an Accuracy of 0.8856. This work provides educational institutions with a precise and robust mechanism to mitigate the risks of compromised authorship, ensuring strict adherence to academic standards.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114656.a: Doctor recommendation in online medical communities (OHCs) is critical for effective patient-doctor matching to address medical needs. However, existing studies face key challenges: inappropriate labels in the training data, an unbounded scope of recommendation targets, and a lack of specialized feature processing for patients' questions. This paper proposes a novel two-phase doctor recommendation approach coordinating deep learning (DL) and reinforcement learning (RL). First, the DL-based triage model generates specialized semantic representations of patients' questions to assign them to appropriate medical departments, thereby narrowing the candidate doctor pool. Second, the deep Q-network-based recommendation model optimizes the reward based on patient-doctor matching information, recommending doctors that meet both patients' clinical consultation needs and subjective satisfaction. Comparative experiments against state-of-the-art baselines on two OHC datasets show that the new triage model outperforms other models by an average of 7.43%p. in accuracy and 10.30%p. in F1-score, while the recommendation model achieves a 38.70% relative increase in average reward and a 6.94%p. improvement in the average user selection rate. Ablation experiments validate the effectiveness of all components. In summary, this work presents a “triage + recommendation” approach that significantly enhances patient-doctor matching performance in OHCs.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114666.a: AbstractTextual disclosures enable scalable, cross-industry measurement of corporate digital activities. Generative Large Language Models (GLLMs) offer contextual understanding, yet prompts introduce subjectivity. We develop a prompt-free GLLM framework to classify digital-related content in Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) sections of annual reports. To ensure measurement reliability, we evaluate two strategies to adapt pre-trained GLLMs for classification: domain-adaptive pre-training (DAPT) to address potential vocabulary gaps, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) to reduce prompt sensitivity. We benchmark these post-training strategies against a BERT baseline using labeled MD&A sentences. Results show that Base-GLLM already encodes sufficient digital vocabulary, rendering DAPT gains marginal. In contrast, PEFT yields substantial improvements and enables prompt-free inference, mitigating prompt subjectivity. The fine-tuned model remains stable under class-imbalance conditions and across firm, industry, and temporal splits. Applying the fine-tuned classifier, we construct a disclosure-based proxy for digital activities. To mitigate cheap-talk concerns, we validate this proxy against observable indicators including digital recruitment and patents. Associations are significant and directionally consistent across policy-shock and matching-based comparability checks. Overall, we provide a prompt-free framework for constructing and validating a disclosure-based measurement artifact of corporate digital activities, enabling objective and reproducible measurement at scale.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114667.a: The extant service quality literature has attested to the positive outcomes of service timeliness, primarily from the customer's perspective, including customer loyalty and satisfaction. With the widespread use of online platforms as a technology-enabled service environment for on-demand services, we expect service timeliness to exert a further influence on critical outcomes from the firm's perspective, particularly some distal outcomes such as restaurant survival. Using empirical evidence from the on-demand food industry in China, we investigate the influence of two time-related factors (i.e., delivery time and delay rate) on the survival of restaurants during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our results confirm that an extended delivery time and a high delay rate reduce the probability of restaurant survival. We further examine the underlying accounts for the effects of the time-related factors on restaurant survival from consumers' post-order decision-making perspective (particularly, their post-order reactions). We reveal that these two factors result in heightened consumer complaints, which subsequently decrease the likelihood of restaurant survival. Unexpectedly, the effects of time-related factors on restaurant survival are not due to consumers' order cancellations. Furthermore, we examine the contingent roles of contextual cues in shaping the effects of time-related factors on consumers' post-order reactions. We find that the positive effect of delivery time on consumer complaints is relatively weaker at high-priced restaurants than at low-priced restaurants, and that the presence of an offline restaurant channel reduces the positive impact of delay on consumer complaints. These nuanced findings advance the literature on service quality in online settings by offering valuable insights into the “distal” effects of service timeliness from the firm's perspective and significant implications for restaurant operations during economic downturns.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114668.a: AbstractUser-generated content (UGC) platforms are characterized by creators producing content and competing for audience attention. As these platforms mature, monetization tools such as sponsored recommendations—which allow creators to pay for enhanced visibility—have become increasingly prominent. However, their implications for platform profitability and creator competition remain unclear, especially in settings where platforms share advertising revenue with creators and where creators can also attract audiences through off-platform promotion. In this paper, we examine UGC platforms' decisions on whether to introduce sponsored recommendations and how to allocate traffic optimally between paid and organic visibility. Using a game-theoretic model, we show that sponsored recommendations are optimal when creators retain a large share of advertising revenue and face high content creation costs. In contrast, when creators receive a smaller revenue share or incur lower marginal effort costs, avoiding sponsored recommendations maximizes platform revenue. We further find that creators invest in platform-based promotion only when paid visibility exceeds a critical threshold, while they consistently pursue off-platform audience acquisition regardless of platform policy. Importantly, although sponsored recommendations can boost short-term platform revenue, excessive reliance on paid promotion reduces content creation effort, weakens off-platform marketing, and limits long-term audience growth. As a result, returns decline for both the platform and creators. Finally, in settings with heterogeneous creators, higher levels of paid visibility further amplify the advantage of high-effectiveness creators in attracting and retaining audiences.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114676.a: Fake news significantly influences decision-making processes by misleading individuals, organizations, and even governments. Large language models (LLMs), as part of generative AI, can amplify this problem by generating highly convincing fake news at scale, posing a significant threat to online information integrity. Therefore, understanding the motivations and mechanisms behind fake news generated by LLMs is crucial for effective detection and governance. In this study, we develop the LLM-Fake Theory, a theoretical framework that integrates various social psychology theories to explain machine-generated deception. Guided by this framework, we design an innovative prompt engineering pipeline that automates fake news generation using LLMs, eliminating manual annotation needs. Utilizing this pipeline, we create a theoretically informed \underline{M}achin\underline{e}-\underline{g}ener\underline{a}ted \underline{Fake} news dataset, MegaFake, derived from FakeNewsNet. Through extensive experiments with MegaFake, we advance both theoretical understanding of human-machine deception mechanisms and practical approaches to fake news detection in the LLM era.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114677.a: Complex societal challenges, such as the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), often manifest as “wicked problems” marked by complexity, ambiguity, and resistance to linear solutions. Addressing such problems demands methodologies that embrace uncertainty and foster and stimulate exploration, reflection, and creativity. Design research (DR) has emerged as a promising approach that bridges theory and practice to facilitate the development of solutions to real-world problems. This paper introduces ORCA, a set of guiding principles to support DR in high-uncertainty contexts, where problems and solutions coevolve. ORCA comprises four interrelated principles: Openness to alternative perspectives, Reflection and reflexivity, a Common communication framework, and Affordance-based design. Drawing on an in-depth analysis of an Action Design Research (ADR) project that led to an operational blockchain-based water exchange aligned with SDG 6 (clean water and sanitation), this paper demonstrates how ORCA enables researchers to navigate and explore uncertainty in design projects tackling wicked, societal challenges and coevolving problem and solution spaces. By integrating effectuation and affordance theory, ORCA provides a structured yet flexible set of guidelines for tackling wicked problems. In doing so, this study advances the evolution of DR methodologies for societal challenges, underscoring the central role of exploration, reflection, and creativity in addressing uncertainty in coevolving problem and solution spaces.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114678.a: Healthcare accessibility is a central social responsibility of healthcare systems. The literature has mainly addressed healthcare shortages from a supply-side perspective by increasing or optimizing healthcare resources. We argue that shortage can also arise from demand-side dynamics, particularly when patients disproportionately prefer higher-ranking physicians, leading to imbalanced demand across physicians. With the increased popularity of online health communities (OHCs), we examine how physician presence in OHCs affect offline patient visits across physician ranks—an institutional signal of professional capability—and the implications for healthcare accessibility. Combining offline data from a top-tier public hospital with online data from China's largest OHC, we employ a difference-in-differences design to examine the offline impact of physician OHC presence. The results show that OHC presence increases offline patient visits, but the effect varies across physician ranks, with higher-ranking physicians attracting larger increases in offline visits than lower-ranking peers. To understand the mechanisms underlying these patterns, we investigated two channels: the advertising effect and the stickiness effect. We find that physician OHC presence attracts new patients visits across all physician ranks but increases returning visits primarily for assistant physicians. Additional analyses show that these gains do not come at the expense of physicians without an OHC presence and that physician OHC presence increases the share of uninsured patients seeking healthcare. Together, our findings indicate that strategically promoting underutilized physicians on OHC may help rebalance patient demand and improve healthcare accessibility without expanding healthcare capacity.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114679.a: Driving data has become a critical input for improving intelligent driving systems, yet firms continue to face data shortages due to high data requirements. To analyze how external data acquisition modes shape competition, we develop a three-spoke model with one dominant firm and two weaker firms. We focus on three scenarios, namely no external data acquisition, data sharing, and data trading, and analyze firms' equilibrium choices. Our results show that data sharing does not necessarily benefit weaker firms. When the dominant firm's product advantage is high, weaker firms choose not to share data, as improvements in autonomous driving performance lead to higher prices and demand losses in markets where they compete with the dominant firm, ultimately reducing their profits. We also find that when the data price is low, all firms participate in data trading, as weaker firms obtain more data and greater autonomous driving performance gains than under data sharing, and the dominant firm earns substantial data revenue. When the data price is high, firms' equilibrium choices once again depend on the dominant firm's product advantage. Moreover, data sharing among weaker firms becomes a key strategic concern for the dominant firm, which has an incentive to proactively engage in data trading to disrupt their cooperation. Finally, we find that consumer surplus may increase or decrease with the dominant firm's product advantage, depending on the data acquisition mode. Our findings highlight the important role of data acquisition strategies in the intelligent driving industry.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114680.a: Model interpretability is increasingly regarded as a core tenet of responsible data science. While there is a growing focus on inherently interpretable ML models, there is still a need for model-agnostic techniques that provide interpretable insights into already-trained ML models. This is particularly important for global interpretability analysis, which characterizes variable effects and interactions across the entire training set. However, existing global interpretability techniques often suffer from long runtimes, model dependence, and a lack of comprehensive and easy-to-implement frameworks. To address this gap, we propose EGIVE (Efficient Global Interaction and Variable Explainability), a framework which allows users to explore a full suite of efficiently-estimated interpretability metrics and visualizations. EGIVE provides importance scores and partial dependence visualizations for single-feature effects, pairwise interactions, and a user-defined set of three-way interactions. By reusing partial-dependence computations and partial dependence inverse propensity weighting to estimate interaction effects EGIVE achieves faster runtimes than baseline implementations in our benchmarks. We demonstrate EGIVE’s ability to recover ground-truth variable effects and interactions in simulated data, and we demonstrate EGIVE’s ability to quickly uncover meaningful clinical patterns using two real-world healthcare datasets.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114681.a: In safety-sensitive industries, AI feedback is increasingly being applied to employee decision-making and performance management. However, existing research has paid limited attention to differences in the institutional embedding of AI feedback and its contextual characteristics, making it difficult to fully understand its application effectiveness. To address these gaps, this study distinguishes between evaluative and non-evaluative AI feedback and introduces the concept of publicness of AI feedback. Grounded in the job demands-resources theory, this study develops a moderated dual-path model to examine how these two types of AI feedback differentially affect employees' safety performance and affective wellbeing, and to test the moderating role of publicness of AI feedback. Based on a quasi-natural experiment with 372 drivers, the findings show that: (1) both types of AI feedback promote safety performance by enhancing role clarity, with evaluative AI feedback exerting a stronger effect; (2) evaluative AI feedback undermines affective wellbeing by increasing perceived job demands, whereas non-evaluative AI feedback directly promotes affective wellbeing; (3) publicness of AI feedback negatively moderates the effects of both feedback types on role clarity and positively moderates the effect of evaluative AI feedback on perceived job demands. This study offers theoretical and practical implications for the design and deployment of AI feedback systems in safety-sensitive industries.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114682.a: Online rumors often circulate before authoritative verification becomes available, requiring users to judge truthfulness under uncertainty. Drawing on Feelings-as-Information Theory, this research examines when emotional arousal carries diagnostic value for truthfulness evaluation in pre-verification rumor settings. Across four experiments (total N = 1010), the findings reveal a conditional pattern in the relationship between emotional arousal and perceived truthfulness. This pattern emerged in a two-stage examination of contextual urgency and in subsequent tests of message framing and social endorsement. Specifically, emotional arousal was more strongly associated with perceived truthfulness in emergency than in general rumor contexts, under negative framing, and under stronger social endorsement. These findings suggest that affective intensity becomes more influential when surrounding cues make it appear interpretable, relevant, and socially corroborated. Theoretically, the research clarifies how affect enters truthfulness evaluation in pre-verification digital environments where external evidentiary anchors are limited at the time of exposure. Practically, the results inform Emotion- and Social-Aware Decision-Support Systems (ES-DSS) that can help users calibrate emotional and social cues against evidentiary quality when evaluating unverified content.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114683.a: Organizations increasingly rely on crowdsourced employee reviews as a source of insight, yet systematic, theory-grounded measures of employee perceptions remain scarce. This study investigates how corporate social responsibility (CSR) relates to employee satisfaction across industries and organizational stigma while introducing DeepEmployee, a deep learning-based decision-support artifact that transforms textual reviews into multidimensional employee perception indicators. Using a thirteen-year panel of employee reviews from a major online platform merged with firm-level CSR indicators, DeepEmployee detects dimensions, such as pride and credibility, grounded in established theoretical frameworks. We find that peripheral CSR concerns reduce employee satisfaction and organizational credibility and weaken the positive effects of employee benefits. The impact of peripheral CSR strengths varies by industry, enhancing employee pride in stigmatized “sin” industries but mattering less than direct benefits in labor-intensive industries. We contribute a scalable, theory-informed deep learning approach to measuring employee perceptions and firm-level evidence on how CSR affects employee attitudes across industries.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114684.a: Early identification of emerging risks from fragmented, noisy evidence remains a central challenge in the Intelligence Phase of decision making, where weak signals must be interpreted under deep uncertainty. We introduce ALERT (Advanced Learning for Early Risk Tracking), a multimodal AI-enabled decision support framework that operationalizes organizational sense-making through evidence triangulation and intelligence augmentation. ALERT integrates social media discourse, biomedical literature, and structured pharmacovigilance data to detect, calibrate, and prioritize candidate adverse side effects (ASEs). Applied to the domain of GLP-1 receptor agonists, ALERT empirically identified 134 ASEs and surfaced 21 novel signals absent from manufacturer labels and established databases. ALERT uncovers a stable logarithmic relationship between social media frequency and validated sources ((Formula presented) ), enabling principled credibility calibration of weak signals. A graph convolutional network captures ASE co-occurrence structure to prioritize risks (F1 = 0.81). Beyond detection, ALERT supports actionable decision support via age-stratified risk profiling ((Formula presented) ) and prediction of treatment discontinuation drivers (F1 = 0.78). Notably, several candidate ASEs initially identified only in social media, including aura-related migraine, ketonemia, and psychiatric effects, were later reported in post-2024 clinical and observational studies, supporting ALERT’s early signal detection capability. This work demonstrates how AI transforms unstructured data into auditable decision cues in uncertain medical and business settings.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114685.a: In the Metaverse era, immersive technologies such as virtual reality (VR) are reshaping collaborations through engaging but complex collaborative virtual environments (CVEs). For this reason, it is essential to identify the key attributes that encourage individuals to use CVEs in such alliances. Grounded in situated cognition theory, this study investigates the key attributes of CVEs and uses trust as a critical mediator to determine how they jointly influence usage intention. First, we identified potential CVE features through a literature review, after which we refined them via a qualitative study to identify those most relevant to usage intention. Building on these insights, we developed a context-specific model that we tested through a sequential quantitative study. Our results reveal a significant interaction between spatial openness and avatar appearance formality in shaping collaboration intention. Importantly, results show that enclosed spaces, especially when paired with formal avatar appearances, enhance perceptions of ability and integrity trust, which in turn positively affect collaboration intention. By clarifying how contextual features shape trust in virtual settings, this study not only explains the underlying mechanisms but also provides practical guidance for designing CVEs through deliberate spatial-avatar configurations.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114686.a: Delegated digital permissions reduce transaction friction but create a distinct security decision problem when authorization and realized loss are temporally decoupled. Drawing on Routine Activity Theory, Protection Motivation Theory, and Technology Threat Avoidance Theory, we examine an Ethereum-based scam centered on malicious permissions, whereby victims grant an allowance that later enables repeated drains without renewed consent, and conceptualize the resulting harm as a post-authorization victimization process shaped jointly by offense opportunity and delayed protective interruption. Using 19,508 scam-related drains from 3514 victim addresses linked to South Korean exchanges between 2021 and 2024, we reconstruct wallet-level trajectories from public-ledger data. Harm is recurrent and time-compressed: 69.4% of victims experience multiple drains; among repeat victims, 22.4% face a second drain within one hour and 30.9% within one day. Within victims, transfer amounts rise with event order while inter-event intervals shrink. An intervention curve shows that immediate mitigation after the first drain could prevent 84.5% of subsequent incident loss, versus 52.2% after seven days. Clustering reveals five victim archetypes, including a sustained high-severity segment comprising 16.2% of victims yet accounting for 80.6% of total loss. Around South Korea's Travel Rule threshold, transfer sizes shift toward sub-threshold execution, consistent with tactical adaptation. The study contributes a victim-trajectory framework for monitoring, triage, and resilient governance in digital ecosystems.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114687.a: On online healthcare platforms, patients struggle to distinguish collective professional patterns from outlier opinions when multiple physicians respond to the same question. We introduce physician-group congruence, which captures the alignment between a focal physician's communication patterns and the collective patterns of co-posted physicians, as a group-level signal that enables patients to assess professional alignment without medical expertise. Analyzing 500,371 physician answers, we find that physician-group congruence significantly increases the likelihood of answer selection, with linguistic style congruence exhibiting the strongest effect, followed by terminology and emotional intensity congruence. At the cross-level, question-answer congruence significantly amplifies the effect of physician-group congruence. Within the group-congruence dimensions, linguistic style and emotional intensity congruence combine synergistically, while terminology congruence serves as an independent credibility filter. A validation study further shows that linguistic style congruence enhances perceived professionalism, which mediates 48.5% of its effect on answer selection, confirming that patients rely on linguistic convergence as a perceptual signal rather than an indicator of medical quality. These findings extend signaling theory to multi-party contexts, suggesting that collective patterns serve as a normative framework for decision-making. Practically, platforms can visualize physician-group congruence alongside credentials to help patients distinguish between mainstream and outlier perspectives, thereby reducing information asymmetry while preserving clinical diversity.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114688.a: Anthropomorphism—defined as the attribution of humanlike characteristics such as identity, verbal and nonverbal behaviors, and other traits to nonhuman agents—plays a pivotal role in alleviating psychological discomfort in human-computer interactions. Although prior research in information systems (IS) has examined anthropomorphism, its development and application within IS and information technology (IT) contexts remain fragmented and underexplored. This study addresses the lack of a cohesive understanding of anthropomorphism in IT/IS environments, where systems are designed, deployed, and used. Drawing on the stimulus–organism–response (S-O-R) framework, we systematically review 195 studies published in leading IS journals, synthesizing existing insights and identifying key gaps. Our findings deepen the theoretical understanding of anthropomorphism in IT/IS and offer actionable guidance for designing humanlike features in digital systems. We conclude by presenting a comprehensive research agenda that outlines critical directions for advancing both theoretical and practical discourse on anthropomorphism in the IT/IS domain.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114696.a: As global demand for accessible mental health solutions grows, AI-driven therapy emerges as a promising alternative for addressing stress-related challenges. Anchored in social cognitive theory (SCT) and the transactional model of stress and coping (TMSC), this study investigates whether AI-mediated interventions can enhance emotional clarity and reduce mental health stigma compared to traditional approaches. Through a three-group experiment comparing AI-guided therapy, human-guided therapy, and journaling, we assess their differential impacts on emotional processing and stress relief. The findings reveal significant improvements across all interventions, with nuanced distinctions emerging. Both human and AI-guided therapies demonstrate superior efficacy over journaling in enhancing emotional clarity, while AI therapy uniquely excels in reducing perceived stigma associated with seeking help. Human and AI modalities show comparable efficacy in promoting adaptive coping strategies, alleviating stress, and increasing future help-seeking intentions, all of which significantly outperform journaling outcomes. Mediation analyses confirm that these effects operate through enhanced emotional clarity and reduced stigma perception. These results substantiate AI's potential as an effective therapeutic tool that reduces stigma and democratizes access to mental health support. The findings offer actionable insights for integrating AI into mental health ecosystems as a complementary or alternative intervention in stress management contexts.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114697.a: A critical pre-requisite to delivering social good through the design of digital solutions is a deep and nuanced understanding of the problem space – beyond awareness, framing or problematization. This “problem of the problem” is particularly acute for wicked psychosocial problems (a subclass of wicked problems) that are characterized by stigma, emotional vulnerability, identity threats, and sensitive disclosure dynamics. In this paper, we develop a set of principles for effective problem space exploration (PSE) for this class of problems. Our work relies on cross-case analysis of PSE journeys for two design science research (DSR) efforts aimed at specific problems in this class: young adults experiencing social anxiety disorder, and older adults facing loneliness. We validate the principles with a retrospective analysis of prior DSR efforts and a structured evaluation from experts to assess their potential applicability. Our work contributes a set of PSE principles for wicked psychosocial problems that are empirically grounded and validated with expert feedback – adding to contemporary discussion of PSE in DSR.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114698.a: Public access to information through open data is critical for achieving the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal 16, which promotes accountable and inclusive institutions. However, open data portals often present barriers, such as complex user interfaces and large data catalogs, that hinder non-technical users from effectively accessing and interpreting the data. To address this problem, we conducted a two-cycle design science research project, guided by the theory of effective use, to design an explainable large language model (LLM)-based open data assistant. After focusing on transparent interaction in the initial design cycle, we evaluated our final artifact through a large-scale online experiment with 223 U.S. citizens using official Texas open data. Our results suggest that while the assistant’s use of natural language enables intuitive access, supplementing answers with explanations of the reasoning process improves citizens’ representational fidelity and effectiveness in finding information. Unexpectedly, we also find that providing a traditional data catalog alongside the conversational interface reduced representational fidelity, suggesting that direct access to raw data may overwhelm citizens. Furthermore, the results show that our design increases perceived government transparency and trust, demonstrating its broader social impact. We synthesize these findings into two design principles for explainable LLM-based open data assistants. Our research contributes to the literature by offering valuable design knowledge for explainable LLM-based systems and by adding novel insights to the discussion about democratizing access to open data. Additionally, we provide practical guidance for implementing LLM-based open data assistants that empower citizens to hold government institutions accountable.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114699.a: The use of generative AI in organizations becomes most apparent when it produces errors. Implementing such systems leads to structural realignments of agency between AI and humans, which, if poorly designed, can result in human workers disengaging from responsibility for work outcomes. This study investigates how collaboration with generative AI systems should be designed to foster human responsibility and reduce errors in AI-augmented work. Adopting a co-creation perspective and drawing on role theory, the research examines how different co-creation designs—human-first versus AI-first and high- versus low-performing AI—shape workers' perceptions of responsibility and their interactions with the generative AI system. An online lab experiment reveals two competing effects: while a human-first approach enhances workers' responsibility, it simultaneously reduces the intensity of co-creation participation when engaging with generative AI; conversely, a high-performing AI diffuses responsibility yet encourages more intense interactions. Building on these findings, the study also provides empirical evidence for the downstream consequences of responsibility, showing that workers' experienced responsibility mitigates errors in work outcomes. These insights advance theory on human-AI co-creation and offer practical design implications for fostering effective and responsible collaboration in AI-augmented work settings.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114700.a: The problem of assessing model misspecification and precision for decision making in areas such as business, cyber security, and medicine remains a pivotal issue. Current state-of-the-art methods in structural equation modeling rely on fixed fit criteria combinations and cut-offs, regardless of model or data characteristics. This approach is often questioned as variations in criteria often depend on these characteristics, raising doubts about the reliability of current decision-making processes and research insights. To address this limitation, we applied a precision-based approach to develop context-specific rules for model assessment and provide them in an easy-to-use Shiny App. This approach is crucial because high precision mitigates the risk of misleading or erroneous insights. Our context-specific rules represent a novel and relevant advancement in model evaluation. They are based on the insight that the performance of criteria combinations depends not only on the characteristics of the data and the model, but also on the specific class of structural equation model employed, such as confirmatory factor analysis or covariance-based structural equation modeling. As a result of our optimization, our developed rules have lower Type I error rates (with an average reduction of almost 50%) than state-of-the-art general combinations while keeping Type II error rates at a low level. Our Shiny App is designed to be user-friendly and accessible, requiring no prior expertise in simulation or programming. This precision-driven, adaptive approach aligns with the goals of decision support systems, which aim to provide context-sensitive insights to support informed, data-driven decisions.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114701.a: Despite its benefits, home-sharing has raised societal concerns about crime. However, research across disciplines has found inconsistent effects of home-sharing on crime. Regarding these inconsistencies, this research examines the temporal dynamics among home-sharing, long-term rental, and various types of crime. We also probe the moderating effects of the local government's short-term rental licensing regulation. We find that the prevalence of home-sharing has a direct positive association with crimes against property in the short term and with crimes against persons in the long term. Through the long-term rental price channel, however, the prevalence of home-sharing has a long-term effect on crimes, leading to higher levels of crimes against property but lower levels of crimes against persons. The licensing regulation mitigates home-sharing's direct adverse impacts on both types of crimes, but the effect becomes insignificant over time. This research contributes to a nuanced understanding of how home-sharing affects crime by delineating both direct effects and effects through the long-term rental channel, as well as their temporal distinctions. We offer practical implications for policymakers, platform operators, hosts, and local communities to promote safer and more sustainable governance of home-sharing.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114702.a: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in the operations of firms. While prior research highlights the value of AI technologies, it often overlooks the collaborative role of humans in shaping firm operational outcomes. Drawing on a multi-source integrated dataset of Chinese firms, this study develops a firm-level measure of human–AI investment synergy and empirically examines its effect on firm operational efficiency. The results indicate that human–AI investment synergy enhances firm operational efficiency by promoting AI-driven innovation. This positive effect is stronger for firms with a more diversified customer base, suggesting that the value of human–AI investment synergy becomes more salient in information-intensive and heterogeneous task environments. The findings further reveal that different configurations of AI human and non-human investments are associated with heterogeneous operational outcomes. In particular, among firms with imbalanced AI resource allocation structures, those with relatively high AI-human and low AI non-human investment exhibit higher operational efficiency than comparable firms with the opposite configuration. Our findings deepen the understanding of the mechanisms through which human–AI collaboration shapes organizational operations and provide practical insights for managers regarding AI resource deployment decisions.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114703.a: Federated learning enables privacy-preserving collaborative modeling and has been widely adopted in data-driven decision-making scenarios such as financial risk management and healthcare analytics. However, its inherent characteristic of “data being available but not visible” introduces a critical vulnerability: malicious participants may manipulate local data or model updates to conduct fraud, thereby degrading model performance and undermining decision reliability. Addressing such fraud is particularly challenging due to limited data transparency, heterogeneous updates, and the lack of interpretable and robust detection mechanisms. To tackle these challenges, this study proposes a novel method, Distributed-Collaborative-Representation-Based Data Fraud Detection (DcrDFD). First, we develop a prototype learning-based representation construction mechanism that transforms participant updates into representative prototypes, enabling interpretable identification of normal, noisy, and fraudulent patterns. Second, we design a multi-variational autoencoder (VAE)-based mutual evaluation mechanism, where prototypes are collaboratively reconstructed and evaluated, significantly enhancing robustness against complex and dynamic data fraud. Third, we introduce a joint optimization framework that integrates fraud detection with federated learning training, enabling dynamic coordination between model learning and fraud prevention. Experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that DcrDFD outperforms state-of-the-art methods in model performance, fraud detection accuracy, and robustness, while maintaining a favorable balance between effectiveness and computational overhead. Overall, this study enhances interpretability, robustness, and reliability in federated learning, providing important implications for secure and trustworthy distributed decision support systems.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114704.a: Mitigating climate change presents significant challenges, particularly in effective carbon stock estimation and planning. Decision-making based on quantified carbon stock is essential for enabling carbon sequestration efforts in natural ecosystems, yet traditional field measurements are labor-intensive, geographically constrained, and difficult to be adopted at scale. Motivated by this practical challenge, we undertook a design science research (DSR) project to develop AI-based decision support systems that enhance the efficiency, accessibility, and scalability for carbon stock estimation and planning. Guided by technology affordance theory, our iterative design, development, demonstration, and evaluation process has led to the conceptualization of four affordance-based design principles that build on and contribute to the growing design knowledge for environmental sustainability. This research advances our understanding of the critical problem and solution domains of carbon stock estimation and planning. It also facilitates the emerging discourse on balancing AI and human intelligence in designing systems for complex decision-making challenges for sustainability. This study provides an exemplar of DSR for supporting Sustainable Development Goal 13 by demonstrating how to design systems that facilitate carbon sequestration and societal transition toward environmental sustainability.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114711.a: Effective mental healthcare typically evolves through an ongoing therapeutic process grounded in sustained physician-patient interactions, where patient revisits play a key role in maintaining such continuity. Nevertheless, empirical research on patient revisits in online mental healthcare settings remains limited. Drawing upon interpersonal trust theory, this study examines whether and how initial physician linguistic style matching (LSM) influences patient revisits in online mental healthcare consultations. Analyzing a large-scale dataset of over 227 thousand real-world consultations from a leading Chinese online healthcare platform, we find a robust, positive association between initial physician LSM and patient revisits. Bootstrapped mediation analysis suggests that this effect operates through a dual trust-building mechanism that fosters both patient affective and cognitive trust. We also observe suggestive evidence of a potential expectation-violation pattern, whereby the positive effect of physician LSM on patient cognitive trust may attenuate at very high levels. Further analyses show that the positive effect of physician LSM is more pronounced when physician responses are more topic-relevant and among patients with milder emotional distress. Finally, the observed effect persists among returning patients and those with chronic physical conditions (e.g., hypertension and diabetes), and physician LSM in publicly visible consultations also serves as a diagnostic signal influencing third-party patient selection. Collectively, our findings advance understanding of patient revisits, physician-patient interactions, and linguistic accommodation in online mental healthcare consultations and provide practical implications to promote effective, patient-centered healthcare.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114712.a: This study develops a conceptual framework of semantic obfuscation in corporate disclosures and proposes a decision support system (DSS) built on large language models (LLMs) to operationalize it at scale. Four dimensions of managerial obfuscation are identified (vagueness, hedging, positive spin, and inconsistency) and scored across more than 16,000 Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) sections from U.S. 10-K filings. The LLM-derived measures are validated through multiple layers of evidence: the measures are highly reproducible across independent scoring runs, consistent with trained human judgments, empirically distinct from traditional readability and tone indices, and predictive of earnings management in theoretically expected directions. In an application to analyst forecasts, the semantic dimensions differentially predict forecast dispersion and accuracy where traditional readability indices do not. The framework advances financial DSS design by positioning generative LLMs as semantic scoring engines capable of transforming unstructured managerial narratives into structured, interpretable signals for analysts, investors, and regulators.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114713.a: A widespread shortage of skilled employees, which also includes the increasing difficulty to retain talented employees by limiting voluntary employee turnover, impedes company success. To gather insights on voluntary employee turnover, previous research has conducted explanatory research focused on theory-driven hypotheses, or utilized predictive models, aiming to predict which employees are most likely to leave the company based on historical data. In contrast, we propose a methodology that combines predictive data mining methods, causal decision trees, and an expert validation to yield firm-specific actionable explanations for employee turnover. The proposed methodology is applied to a real-world case of a mechanical engineering company. Here, our data-driven causal analysis identifies patterns of voluntary service technician turnover, which are validated by domain experts and used to derive targeted measures for reducing future employee turnover. The results are shown to provide valuable insights, adding to the a priori knowledge of the experts, revealing discrepancies between subjective opinions and quantitative results, and substantially informing the company's decision-making. A follow-up study demonstrates that almost all of the derived measures are being realized and indicates early positive effects on employee turnover.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114714.a: High-involvement product recommendation, due to its high value and high perceived risks, often leads to user preference shifts during multi-turn conversations, exacerbating issues such as the inherent instability of large language model (LLM)-based conversational recommender systems (CRS), thus posing challenges for existing CRS. To fill this research gap, we focus on high-involvement product recommendation scenario and develop a multi-agent recommender framework that integrates both reflection and critique. By designing a Reflector agent that reflects on user feedback at the user decision-making level, it promptly captures user preference instability and updates system strategies; by designing two Critic agents that monitor system responses in real-time, it mitigates the problem of unstable system generation. Overall, through multi-agent collaboration, the framework addresses the inherent user preference instability in this scenario. Experiments on a real-world product dataset from the automotive domain demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, additional experiments show that in scenarios characterized by severe preference instability, our model still achieves higher recommendation accuracy, while in scenarios with stable user preferences, it can complete recommendations in fewer dialogue turns. Its effectiveness in the high-involvement product recommendation scenario demonstrates its practical application potential.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114715.a: Service failures are inevitable in chatbot-based customer service. In hybrid customer service systems, when a chatbot fails, a human agent typically takes over and resume service for the customer. However, little is known about how to effectively initiate this transition from chatbot failure to human-agent intervention. This study identifies four initiation methods varying in service proactivity: passive initiation, text prompt initiation, button prompt initiation, and automatic initiation. Extending social information processing theory with a cognitive decision perspective, we develop a theoretical framework to examine how consumers attribute the observed initiation methods to organizational motives, which subsequently influence their satisfaction. We conduct three online experiments to examine how these initiation methods influence recovery satisfaction, as well as the underlying psychological mechanisms and boundary conditions. The results reveal significant differences in recovery satisfaction across initiation methods, mediated by customers' inferred selfish intent. Furthermore, compared with low task urgency, high task urgency significantly amplifies differences in recovery satisfaction and inferred selfish intent among various human-agent initiation methods. These findings advance understanding of recovery strategies for chatbot service failures, offering actionable guidance for designing effective transitions from chatbots to human agents in hybrid service settings.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114716.a: While firms largely rely on inter-organizational information and resources to make corporate social responsibility (CSR) decisions, very few studies have delved into the heterogeneous effects of different categories of board networks. Through adopting a large language model (LLM) as an analytical tool to transform unstructured resumes into structured decision-relevant intelligence, we fulfill this research gap by constructing in-depth board networks with three distinct types: current network, past network, and non-profit organization network. Based on a dataset of Chinese listed firms from 2011 to 2020, we empirically estimate whether and how firms connected through board networks would result in CSR performance similarity. The results show that the existence and heterogeneity of board networks are positively associated with CSR performance similarity between interlocked firms. Interestingly, our findings reveal that other than current networks, past networks, and non-profit networks have a higher impact on the CSR performance similarity. Further analysis suggests that the positive association between social networks and CSR performance similarity is attenuated when connected firms face higher media coverage and higher analyst coverage. Overall, this study provides insightful evidence to leverage the effect of board networks, informing decision support for investors, regulators, and corporate strategists by revealing hidden network drivers of CSR-related decisions.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114717.a: Credit card fraud detection remains a significant challenge due to extreme class imbalance, evolving fraud patterns, and asymmetric costs of misclassification. While existing machine learning methods often prioritize fraud detection performance, they frequently overlook model risk management, which is crucial for reliable decision making in high-stakes environments. To address this issue, we introduce DISCO—a framework that combines discriminative and robust representation learning with a conformal prediction-based mechanism for provable risk control. At its core, DISCO is established upon the principle of decoupling representation learning from risk-controlled decision-making. To this end, we first leverage deep metric learning (DML) to construct an embedding space that is inherently robust to class imbalance and resilient to concept drift. Subsequently, we employ a conformal risk control (CRC) mechanism to provide a formal statistical guarantee on the false negative rate (FNR) of the resulting model according to a user-specified FNR target. Computational experiments on a real-world dataset demonstrate that DISCO outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both classification performance and operational efficiency. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to integrate a DML-based representation learning with a formal risk control mechanism for reliable credit card fraud detection. The proposed framework therefore offers a trustworthy and practical solution that addresses the dual imperatives of predictive performance and reliability.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114718.a: Electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM) plays a critical role in shaping consumer decisions and influencing product sales. While prior research has extensively examined the relationship between aggregate eWOM metrics, such as valence and volume, and sales, less is known about how aspect-level eWOM sentiment relates to overall ratings and market outcomes. This study leverages large language models (LLMs) to extract fine-grained aspect-specific sentiment from online reviews and examines the relationships among multi-aspect sentiment, overall ratings, and product sales. Using data from the movie industry, we develop an LLM-based framework to identify sentiment toward plot, cast, director, and audiovisual, and empirically test their associations with ratings and box office using ridge regression. The findings show that plot sentiment has the strongest positive association with box office, followed by cast and director sentiment. Audiovisual sentiment is positively associated with overall ratings, but its relationship with box office is more context-dependent. Overall ratings partially mediate the effects of plot, cast, and director sentiment, and overall ratings, sentiment dispersion, and cross-aspect sentiment interactions further condition aspect-level effects. This research contributes to the eWOM literature by offering a fine-grained understanding of how multi-aspect sentiment relates to market outcomes and provides practical insights for managing online movie reputation.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114719.a: The rapid rise of short-form video commerce has posed new challenges for accurate sales prediction. Previous studies often overlook the sequential features and temporal structure of modality-specific data. Our main contribution is to develop a signal-driven multimodal sequence fusion (SMSF) framework grounded in signaling theory. SMSF employs a hierarchical attention-based fusion strategy that combines self-attention, pairwise cross-modal attention, and joint attention to enhance sequential modeling and enable effective representation of complex and heterogeneous multimodal signals beyond conventional fusion methods. All enhanced signals are fused via dynamic gating for adaptive modality selection, followed by a Mixture-of-Experts module that improves semantic coordination. We use a multimodal dataset of 8084 short-form sales videos from Douyin (TikTok in China) for experiments. The results indicate that SMSF consistently outperforms benchmark models. Ablation experiments further reveal that online comments contribute most to prediction performance. Its signal processing and enhancement methods provide a potential paradigm for multimodal tasks across different scenarios or platforms.

Stephan Kuehnel: Writing – review & editing, Methodology, Conceptualization, Data curation, Visualization, Validation, Funding acquisition, Supervision. Johannes Damarowsky: Conceptualization, Funding acquisition, Supervision.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114721.a: This study investigates whether explainable AI (XAI), although intended to improve calibrated reliance in augmented decision-making (ADM), may also increase negative consultations. In a between-subjects online experiment ( n = 200), participants completed a price classification task supported by AI, while we manipulated the presence of local feature-based explanations. Drawing on dual-process theory as an interpretive lens, we conceptualize explainability as a cognitively ambivalent intervention that reshapes reliance behavior. Our results show that XAI-induced transparency exerts competing effects: while it directly reduces negative consultations, it simultaneously increases competence-based trust and shifts responsibility attribution toward the AI. These mechanisms foster overreliance and significantly increase negative consultations, resulting in a competitive mediation pattern. Notably, comparable effects do not emerge for positive consultations, suggesting that transparency more readily amplifies reliance than it promotes corrective belief updating. By empirically demonstrating this paradox, our study develops IS and Decision Sciences research on automation bias in transparent ADM settings and identifies key psychological mechanisms through which explainability influences reliance. These findings inform the design of XAI systems that prioritize calibrated reliance rather than merely increasing perceived transparency.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114722.a: Immersive technologies across extended reality (xR), including virtual reality, augmented reality, and mixed reality, are reshaping how individuals and organizations represent, experience, and act upon digital information. Yet information systems research on immersive technologies remains fragmented across technology categories, theoretical perspectives, application domains, and levels of analysis, limiting cumulative theory development. This study synthesizes 252 immersive-technology studies from leading IS journals and conferences to examine how this fragmented literature can be integrated. Our analysis reveals that, although prior studies appear diverse at the surface level, they increasingly converge around two interrelated analytical layers. First, higher-order mechanisms, including affordance-based, dynamic/temporal, tension-based, social/identity, and signal/data-driven mechanisms, shape how immersive environments structure, coordinate, constrain, balance, adapt, and personalize human–technology interaction across contexts and over time. Second, foundational experiential processes, including perceptual, cognitive, and affective processes, constitute the proximal pathways through which immersive systems influence environmental perception, information processing, emotional engagement, behavior, and outcomes. Building on these insights, we develop a mechanism-centered framework that reconceptualizes immersive systems not as isolated technology categories, but as configurations that generate nonlinear, contingent, and multi-level outcomes through the interaction of higher-order mechanisms and foundational experiential processes. By shifting the analytical focus from technology categories to mechanism-centered explanation, this study provides an integrated foundation for cumulative theory development and advances understanding of immersive systems as adaptive, experience-mediated information systems. We conclude by outlining a research agenda for future immersive systems research in IS and for the design of next-generation immersive decision support systems.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114723.a: Stock prediction in financial markets aims to forecast stock trends and prices, which is crucial for achieving profitable investments. Traditional methods primarily involve modeling and predicting based on stock time-series data. Although many recent studies have incorporated contextual signals such as financial events, corporate disclosures, and investor sentiment, existing forecasting models often use such information mainly as predictive inputs rather than as evidence for post-hoc forecast correction. As a result, baseline forecasts may remain over-dependent on historical data distributions and become misaligned with current market conditions in uncertain decision-making processes. In contrast, large language models (LLMs), as decision models driven by rich knowledge, are powerful tools that can help us construct such correction mechanisms. We propose SPCE, a Post-Hoc Expert Correction framework decoupling trend extrapolation from causal reasoning. First, it adopts a correction-over-training paradigm where LLMs refine baseline forecasts without retraining. Second, a Knowledge-Guided mechanism mitigates forecast bias by grounding corrections in dynamic financial knowledge graphs and real-time sentiment. Third, a Regime-Adaptive Multi-Agent strategy orchestrates specialized LLMs, fusing their outputs via meta-cognitive consistency checks to ensure robust, context-aware predictions in volatile markets. Experiments conducted on three benchmark datasets, CMIN-US, StockNet, and CMIN-CN, show that SPCE achieves average reductions of 7.2% in RMSE, 8.9% in MAE, and 9.3% in MAPE compared with the CNN-BiLSTM-Attention baseline. The results highlight its effectiveness in volatile and heterogeneous market environments, positioning SPCE as a scalable and adaptable decision support mechanism for financial forecasting.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114731.a: Online knowledge platforms have become essential infrastructures for digital knowledge creation and exchange, yet sustaining user knowledge contributions remains a persistent challenge due to high cognitive demands and limited social incentives. This challenge has been further intensified by the widespread adoption of generative AI (GenAI). To address this issue, many platforms have introduced social post features that encourage informal, socially driven content sharing. This study investigates how social post features affect user knowledge contributions and whether they mitigate the adverse effects of GenAI. First, leveraging a large-scale panel dataset of over 10,000 user activity records, this study exploits the platform's rollout of the “idea” feature—a social post function—as an exogenous policy shock and employs a Difference-in-Differences (DID) approach within a quasi-experimental framework. The DID analysis results indicate that the introduction of social post features significantly increases knowledge contributions. Further analysis of the underlying mechanisms reveals that this effect operates primarily through enhanced self-disclosure, increased social interaction, and improved task decomposability. Furthermore, using an interrupted time-series analysis based on the release of ChatGPT as an exogenous GenAI shock, we find that while GenAI generally reduces user knowledge contributions, users who actively engage in social posts experience significantly smaller declines, indicating that socially oriented design features can effectively buffer the negative impacts of GenAI. Our findings offer theoretical insights and practical guidance for sustaining user engagement and maintaining resilient knowledge ecosystems in the GenAI era.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114732.a: Bundle recommendation is a widely used marketing strategy designed to suggest related items to users, providing users with one-stop convenience while increasing platform efficiency. Yet, aligning bundle recommendations with user preferences remains challenging due to the complex tripartite relationships among users, bundles, and items. This challenge is further exacerbated by sparse user–bundle interactions, where the large number of bundles and limited user engagements hinder accurate preference estimation and often result in suboptimal outcomes. To address these issues, we propose an advanced multi-graph contrastive framework powered by large language models (LLMs). The framework integrates multi-view expansion and LLM-based data augmentation to enrich interaction signals, while employing multi-graph contrastive learning to improve the accuracy and robustness of representation learning. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across overall performance and varying sparsity conditions, underscoring its effectiveness across three benchmark real-world datasets. Moreover, the observed alignment between sparse and dense users with similar preferences suggests that the LLM-enhanced augmentation enables the model to learn meaningful representations even under sparse settings.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114733.a: As privacy concerns intensify and data regulations become increasingly stringent, ad-supported platforms are adopting distinct privacy protection models to balance advertising revenue with consumers’ privacy expectations. This paper develops an analytical framework to compare three prevalent models: the traditional model, in which platforms unconditionally collect consumer data and expose users to advertisements; the subscription model, which offers users an opt-out option by paying a fee to avoid both data collection and advertising; and the data compensation model, which provides monetary incentives to users who voluntarily share their personal data. Our model specifically examines an ad-supported platform’s decisions regarding the optimal privacy protection model and data collection intensity for consumers exhibiting heterogeneous privacy sensitivity. Our analysis identifies the conditions under which each model becomes the platform’s profit-maximizing choice and examines how these choices impact social welfare and consumer surplus. We find that when the intensity of privacy infringement is high, the subscription model is optimal for the platform; whereas when the privacy infringement is low, the data compensation model yields the highest platform profits; otherwise, the traditional model outperforms the other models. Furthermore, while all three models can achieve maximum social welfare, only the data compensation model has the potential to create a win-win outcome for both the platform and consumers. In contrast, the subscription and traditional models often enhance platform profits at the expense of consumer welfare. These findings provide theoretical and policy insights for designing effective privacy strategies in content platforms.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114734.a: Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered chatbots are becoming increasingly popular, with users engaging these chatbots to obtain information or to “socialize.” While previous research has considered the mechanisms governing user adoption of chatbots at a macro level, the underlying micro-level logic remains vague. Based on signal theory and dual-process theory, we propose a research model elucidating the signaling role of linguistic features in chatbot responses during user–chatbot interactions. Particularly, we focus on three linguistic signals: informative, affective, and matching signals, and investigate their impact on user adoption at the message level of interactions. The research model is empirically analyzed using chat logs collected from an online AI chat platform hosted in the United States that documents interactions between users and AI chatbots. According to the results, all three signals significantly influence users' adoption of chatbot responses—albeit with directionally variant effects. Furthermore, certain signals are moderated by user expertise and task complexity. Overall, this study both enriches our understanding of linguistic signals during human–AI interaction and affords practical insights regarding the improvement of AI chatbots.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114735.a: We propose the Expert-Augmented Semantic Embedding (EASE) weighting scheme, which integrates domain knowledge into machine learning-based sentiment analysis of corporate disclosures. EASE leverages the Loughran and McDonald financial sentiment lexicon to geometrically define a semantically meaningful direction in a word embedding space, enabling continuous and graded sentiment scoring of the full lexicon, including words absent from the original lexicon, without requiring labeled outcome data or model retraining. Using a large sample of 10-K annual reports, we show that EASE-augmented sentiment measures exhibit improved economic significance and explanatory power for market returns and future earnings relative to their non-augmented counterparts. Because EASE anchors sentiment weights to an expert-defined semantic axis rather than to historically observed outcomes, the resulting measures are potentially less susceptible to the influence of strategically deployed or otherwise shifting language in corporate disclosures. Our findings highlight the complementarity between human knowledge and machine learning in extracting economically meaningful sentiment from financial texts.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114736.a: Financial market segmentation has predominantly relied on supply-based methods that emphasize the corporate business market, while paying scarce attention to demandoriented schemes that highlight shared investor preferences and behaviors. This study narrows this gap by proposing an investor demand-oriented approach for financial market segmentation, which consists of three fundamental phases: financial network construction based on investor co-attention, network representation learning using network embedding techniques, and clustering over network embeddings. By implementing the approach in the U.S. stock market and cross-validating its usefulness in the Chinese stock market, we first show that it can reflect pairwise stock similarity, as network embedding similarity is significantly and positively associated with excess comovement between stocks. We then partition the stock market into different peer groups that demonstrate significant within-group comovement. The utility and efficacy of our approach are comprehensively evaluated by comparing it with traditional industry classifications, geographical location-based classification, text-based classification, and search cluster-based investment habitats. The results demonstrate that our approach not only achieves better performance in capturing greater withingroup homogeneity and between-group heterogeneity, but also outperforms standard classification schemes in predicting excess comovement and stock returns. This study adds to design science research on financial market segmentation by extending the important yet underexplored domain of demand-oriented methods. By systematically decoding latent investor preferences and behavioral commonalities, our approach can be integrated into automated decision support systems to improve the accuracy and efficiency of financial market analytics pragmatically.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114737.a: Social recommendation leverages users’ social network information to enhance product recommendation. To mitigate the issue of low-quality social signals, prior studies have introduced graph denoising and graph disentanglement. However, due to the lack of strong supervision, these methods often yield suboptimal performance. In this study, we propose a new framework for explicit semantic disentanglement. Specifically, we first use a Large Language Model (LLM) to extract user intentions from reviews and construct intention-specific collaborative subgraphs, which serve as supervision signals to disentangle the social graph into multiple intention-specific social subgraphs. This enables the model to independently learn interaction and social signals under different intentions. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and explainability.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114738.a: Operational risk plays a critical role in the management of construction projects. In particular, when complicated machinery is involved, failure to effectively monitor such risks can lead to severe accidents and project delays. Machine learning presents a promising solution to this engineering challenge. However, due to the inherent heterogeneity across construction projects, leveraging historical project data for risk prediction in target projects remains a significant challenge. In this study, we design a multimodal transfer learning framework to predict variations in engineering-machinery operations from plans. To select appropriate source projects for knowledge transfer, we consider both the similarity between source and target projects (built up on project management documentation and operational data) and the importance of source projects within the project similarity network. Our model also integrates multimodal information to strengthen its predictive capability. We evaluate our approach on real-world shield tunnel boring machine projects and demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models. Our results indicate that the framework serves as a practical and effective tool for improving the management of complex engineering projects.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114739.a: Although integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into work processes is often expected to enhance productivity, such transformation may also undermine employee satisfaction, which is essential for the long-term success of AI adoption. As organizations implement various modalities of human–AI collaboration, it remains unclear how these arrangements affect employee satisfaction. This paper addresses this gap by delineating three distinct collaboration modalities: human-led, AI-led, and co-led. We examine how each modality influences user satisfaction with collaborative outcomes and collaborative processes, and how these effects vary across task environments. Our findings show that when task uncertainty is low, the human-led modality leads to higher outcome satisfaction; however, as uncertainty increases, differences in outcome satisfaction across modalities diminish. In contrast, process satisfaction remains consistently sensitive to collaboration modality regardless of task uncertainty, and this effect is further amplified by task complexity. Across all conditions, the AI-led modality produces the highest levels of process satisfaction. Moreover, we also reveal a tension between satisfaction and performance. Although the co-led modality produces lower satisfaction with both the outcome and the process, it achieves the highest decision quality. By shifting attention from collaboration performance alone to collaboration satisfaction, this study extends research on human–AI collaboration and offers practical guidance for designing AI-based work processes that support both effectiveness and sustainability.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114740.a: Recommender systems significantly improve the quality and confidence of consumer decisions by alleviating information overload through streamlined retrieval, playing a vital role in e-commerce platforms. However, most recommender systems underutilize contextual information and fail to explicitly model users’ cognitive processes, leading to biased preference learning. Drawing on information foraging theory, this study adopts the design science research methodology to develop Tiresias, a framework that aligns with users’ cognitive processes by mimicking how proximal cues and foraging costs are assessed for each product. Proximal cues such as product category and affinitive relationships, and foraging costs such as behavior type, dwell time, and foraging progression, are identified and encoded as learnable features. To model the product-foraging journey, Typhon is designed as a Kolmogorov–Arnold network-enhanced differential transformer with a non-invasive feature injection mechanism. A multi-task learning objective that combines next-product prediction with auxiliary cue and cost prediction refines contextualized preference representations. Experiments on datasets show that Tiresias achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming baselines by up to 5.44%. Finally, post-hoc analysis reveals learned representation patterns consistent with dynamic preference evolution throughout the user’s product foraging journey. Methodologically, the study demonstrates how information foraging theory can guide feature selection, feature learning, and objective design. Practically, the study offers actionable insights for developing cognitive process-aware recommender systems that better support consumer decision-making.

10.1016/j.dss.2026.114741.a: Despite the importance of aesthetics in peer-to-peer (P2P) accommodation, prior studies have neither integrated rhetoric into the multimodal information framework nor examined the synergistic or antagonistic effects between rhetoric aesthetics and image aesthetics. To address this gap, this study employs text mining and image detection techniques to operationalize aesthetics as rhetoric aesthetics and image aesthetics, with the latter further comprising cover image aesthetics and sleep space image aesthetics. Based on aesthetic arousal theory, this study uses secondary data from 20,144 Airbnb listings to construct econometric models and conducts four scenario-based experiments. The results indicate that rhetoric aesthetics has an inverted U-shaped effect on customers' booking intentions, mediated by aesthetic pleasure—that is, rhetoric aesthetics exerts an inverted U-shaped effect on aesthetic pleasure, which in turn positively influences customers' booking intentions. Cover image aesthetics enhances the inverted U-shaped effect of rhetoric aesthetics and its indirect effect, whereas sleep space image aesthetics weakens both.
