10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103621.a: Academic spin-offs (ASOs) are widely recognized for their innovation premium, originating from the transfer of novel academic knowledge and superior innovative capacities. However, their innovation patterns after achieving the sustainable returns phase remain underexplored. To understand the temporal dynamics of their innovation strategies, we focus on mature ASOs using a sample of Chinese publicly listed firms from 2008 to 2020. We find that mature ASOs exhibit a stronger propensity for exploitative innovation over exploratory innovation when compared with their non-academic counterparts. Moreover, this tendency is amplified by greater external institutional investment, but mitigated by a greater proportion of non-academic team members and greater internal financial slack. Overall, this study advances research on ASO innovation by clarifying how ASOs leverage their innovative advantage in the sustainable returns phase, as well as highlighting the continuing importance of commercial resources in shaping mature ASOs’ innovation propensity.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103622.a: Innovation tournaments require expert evaluators to assess large volumes of lengthy, unstructured proposals under significant time pressure and cognitive constraints. This study investigates how transformer-based natural language processing (NLP) models can be integrated into this context as decision-support tools within the evaluation process. Using real-world data from a national Brazilian innovation tournament comprising 1151 startup proposals, we examine whether NLP models can learn patterns associated with expert-assigned scores and support early-stage screening. We fine-tune Portuguese-language transformer models (BERT) for classification tasks and refine long-text processing through chunking and document-level aggregation. To contextualize performance, we benchmark the neural models against lighter architectures and classical machine-learning baselines. Although the models exhibit persistent ambiguity in distinguishing intermediate-quality proposals, the best-performing configuration consistently avoids extreme misclassifications and adopts a conservative screening profile that prioritizes the retention of high-potential submissions.

The authors would like to apologise for any inconvenience caused.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103625.a: Despite substantial investments in big data analytics by manufacturing firms, how these investments translate into business value remains poorly understood. Drawing on resource orchestration theory (ROT) and insights from the big data literature, we examine how improving resource bundling (IRB) and pioneering resource bundling (PRB) mediate the impact of big data analytics on firm performance and the moderating role of servitization in these relationships. Analyzing a dataset of 322 Chinese manufacturers, we find that both IRB and PRB serve as mediators for the positive effect of big data analytics on firm performance. Interestingly, servitization strengthens the positive relationship between big data analytics and IRB while weakening its positive relationship with PRB, illustrating a double-edged effect. This study advances the literature in several streams, including big data analytics, servitization, and resource orchestration.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103626.a: Twin transition, the concurrent development of digitalization practices and circular practices, are believed to be the key to firm performance. However, empirical evidence is currently scarce regarding the effect of twin transition on firm performance and the complementary practices that enable and realize it. This study draws on a survey of 188 Swedish manufacturing firms and employs PLS structural equation modelling to test the hypothesis. The results indicate that firm performance can be improved through digitalization practices but with circular practices as a mediator. Moreover, our results show a significant and positive moderation effect of supply chain orchestration and supply chain business model innovation as complementary mechanisms for enabling and realizing the process. This implies time sequencing between the two twin transition dimensions. These results carry theoretical implications for twin transition research and circular economy literatures. The results also provide novel managerial insights by showing that digital investments must be coupled with early orchestration of supply chain partners and aligned business model innovation to effectively scale circular practices and realize performance benefits.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103627.a: In the current digital era, manufacturing firms are increasingly pursuing servitization to enhance competitive advantage. Nevertheless, the mechanisms linking digital technology adoption (DTA) to servitization remain underexplored. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities perspective (DCP) and ecosystem perspective, this study develops a conceptual model to examine how DTA is associated with servitization through knowledge coupling and under what conditions this relationship is amplified or constrained. Utilizing data from 925 listed Chinese manufacturing firms over the 2010–2024 period, we employ a two-way fixed effects model to show that DTA is positively associated with servitization, with knowledge coupling serving as a critical mediating pathway. Furthermore, we identify that collaborative network cohesion plays an inverted U-shaped moderating role on the DTA–knowledge coupling relationship, highlighting the importance of an optimally structured ecosystem for effective knowledge integration. These findings advance theoretical understanding of digital-enabled servitization and provide actionable insights for managers seeking to leverage digital technologies and ecosystem networks to facilitate service-oriented transformation.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103628.a: In the digital era, as enterprises increasingly embrace a variety of digital technologies to drive innovation and alleviate operational pressures, the key challenge has evolved from simple technology adoption to the strategic selection and integration of these technologies for achieving optimal results. Although previous literature has examined the factors contributing to heterogeneous digital innovation outcomes, most studies focusing on the independent effects of these factors fail to fully capture the causal complexity underlying digital innovation. Drawing on digital technology affordance theory, this study addresses this gap by adopting a configurational approach based on the “Technology-Organization-Goal” (T-O-G) framework. Using data from 2151 listed manufacturing companies in China that participate in digital innovation, the study employs fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to identify configurations that generate high levels of digital innovation. The findings demonstrate that differences in innovation performance do not arise from isolated factors, but from the actualization of affordances enabled by the synergistic alignment of technology, organization, and goals. Crucially, we show that affordance actualization is not an automatic outcome but hinges on specific configurations. Furthermore, we highlight that the conversion of technological potential into value is strictly governed by the alignment between an organization's structural attributes and its strategic intent. Finally, by revealing equifinal pathways to successful digital innovation rather than a one-size-fits-all solution, our findings provide managers with actionable guidance.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103629.a: Digital platforms have become a dominant logic for value creation and innovation, yet legacy firms still struggle to translate platform principles into actionable organizational transformation. A central reason is cognitive: managers often mis-frame platforms as digital services rather than as ecosystem-based value architectures. This paper adopts a Design Science approach to develop and refine the Platform Thinking Journey, a composite managerial artifact that supports platform transformation in incumbent firms. Developed through a three-year, multi-firm collaboration within the Platform Thinking HUB, the artifact evolved across three iterative waves from exploratory tools into a validated journey structured around four phases: Framing, Design, Ignition, and Growth. The resulting Platform Thinking Journey combines a process model, bounded decision cycles, and an integrated physical and digital, or “phygital”, support architecture, including cards, canvases, workshops, digital templates, and a GenAI co-thinker. Its core mechanism is to make platform theory actionable by presenting structured alternatives grounded in the literature, focusing managerial attention, reducing ambiguity, and aligning interpretation before teams consolidate choices through design tools and milestones. The study contributes to platform and innovation management research by showing how platform transformation can be actively supported through design, and by identifying five design principles for incumbent firms: reframing from products to interactions before solutioning, structuring the process as bounded decision cycles, materializing reasoning through boundary objects, balancing conceptual depth with cognitive manageability, and sustaining reflection through phygital continuity. Methodologically, the paper offers a rigorous application of Design Science to a non-technical managerial artifact in a multi-wave, multi-firm collaborative setting. For managers, the Platform Thinking Journey provides a structured way to reframe platform opportunities, make key design choices explicit, and sustain reflection across the transformation process.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103630.a: Industrial parks have become important sites for university–industry collaboration (UIC), yet existing research offers limited explanation of why particular UIC models emerge, evolve, and work unevenly across institutional contexts. This study develops a hierarchical multi-level framework in which field embeddedness shapes institutional linkages and Actor Endowments, which in turn condition UIC model selection. Using survey data from 412 respondents across 16 Chinese industrial parks and comparative case evidence from four focal parks, supplemented by RTP as an international reference, we identify four analytically ordered UIC models: talent exchange, technology transfer, value co-creation, and ecosystem symbiosis. The SEM results show that Actor Endowments exert the strongest direct association with UIC model selection (β = 0.482, p < 0.001), whereas field embeddedness operates mainly through indirect pathways via institutional linkages and Actor Endowments. These mechanisms vary across park types and regional development levels. The study contributes to UIC research by explaining model differentiation and progressive upgrading through a contextualized multi-level framework, offering implications for policy, park management, and collaborative practice.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103631.a: As sustainability improvement becomes increasingly complex and uncertain, firms are increasingly dependent on networked innovation capability to integrate dispersed knowledge and technologies from external entities. However, the transformation from networked innovation capability to sustainability involves a procedural mechanism that requires effective synergy among limited multidimensional financial and digital resources. This procedural mechanism and the role of resource synergy within it remain underexplored. Based on network embeddedness theory, innovation value chain theory, and resource synergy theory, this study constructs an integrated “Networked Innovation Capabilities-Process-Resources” synergy framework and employs stepwise regression analysis on a sample of 165 new energy vehicle firms. Results show that: (1) Networked knowledge innovation capability promotes sustainability through a procedural mechanism involving networked technology innovation capability and market value. (2) Multidimensional financial resources exert heterogeneous effects across different links of the procedural mechanism, with financial leverage and profitability showing significantly positive moderating effects, while operational efficiency shows no significant effect. (3) Multidimensional digital resources exert dual supportive or exhausting influences on the synergistic effects of financial resources, where digital development orientation provides consistent support, whereas digital software and hardware investment exhibit both supportive and exhausting effects contingent upon the specific link of the procedural mechanism. This study elucidates how networked innovation capability affects sustainability through a procedural mechanism and how diverse yet limited resources synergize in this process. It provides theoretical and practical insights for firms and governments to promote networked innovation capability and optimize the allocation of financial and digital resources in innovation process for sustainability.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103632.a: Collaborative innovation is crucial in addressing complex challenges such as sustainability-oriented and technological transformation. While previous research has explored the mechanisms and outcomes of collaborative innovation, scholars and practitioners still lack clear, actionable guidance on how to design, select, adapt, and evaluate the tools and methods—referred to as artifacts—that support the collaborative innovation process. This paper addresses that question. Drawing on an Action Design Research (ADR) study across three cases and five iterative build-intervene-evaluate cycles, we develop the Orchestrating Collaborative Innovation (OCI) methodological framework. Grounded in a process perspective, organization theory, and empirical insights, OCI introduces 18 phase-specific design principles for innovation community participants and 10 for orchestrators to guide artifact development. OCI is a methodological framework for design science scholars and innovation orchestrators. It supports scholars and practitioners in designing, adapting, and selecting artifacts that align with a specific phase of the collaborative innovation process and evaluating them accordingly. By doing so, the innovation community can become more cohesive, align on shared goals, and co-create innovation. Beyond collaborative innovation, the framework contributes to advancing a process perspective in design science by emphasising the evolving, relational, and performative nature of the innovation process.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103633.a: While reverse engineering is widely recognized as a key mechanism for emerging market firms to acquire sophisticated knowledge for product innovation, it faces distinctive challenges when applied to digital products due to their layered modular architecture. Substantial portions of digital product functionality reside in unobservable layers such as algorithms, data, and backend services, limiting the completeness of knowledge that reverse engineering can capture. Drawing on layered modular architecture literature, we propose that rapid validity testing serves as an important bridging mechanism that transforms the incomplete knowledge from reverse engineering into more comprehensive and actionable insights for digital product innovation. Using multi-wave survey data from 286 Chinese manufacturing firms, we find that reverse engineering is positively associated with digital product innovation in emerging market firms, and rapid validity testing mediates this relationship. We also find that the indirect effect is positively moderated by firms’ knowledge integration capability. This study advances understanding of how emerging market firms leverage acquired architectural knowledge to overcome the observability constraints commonly encountered in digital product innovation, and illuminates the organizational processes through which such knowledge is transformed into genuine innovation capability.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103634.a: This paper examines the relationship between digital mergers and acquisitions (M&As) and acquisition premiums in the context of China's rapidly evolving digital economy. Based on 4761 acquisition events of A-share listed firms from 2011 to 2022, we find that digital M&As significantly increase acquisition premiums. Evidence from patent-based identification points towards digital capabilities driving premium formation. Further analysis reveals that acquiring firms' management digital technology background strengthens the positive effect of digital M&As on premiums, while their digital transformation levels weaken this relationship. The effect is more pronounced in conglomerate acquisitions than in horizontal or vertical acquisitions. Additional tests show that digital M&A premiums reduce agency costs and enhance market value, particularly for firms with high absorption capacity, though they may crowd out future digital innovation. Our findings suggest that digital resource scarcity and expectations of synergistic value creation drive firms' willingness to pay premiums in digital acquisitions.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103635.a: To provide firms with frontier solutions for fulfilling their social responsibilities, our study attempts to approach corporate green innovation from the novel angle of value (in)congruence of patent pledges. Patent pledges, as an important corporate financing source, entail a dual value portfolio comprising both technological and exclusionary values. However, seldom studies have examined how the dynamic (im)balance state between the two value forms of patent pledges drives firms' strategic actions such as green innovation. Using a longitudinal panel dataset that contains 86,961 patent records of 3011 Chinese manufacturing firms during 2012-2021, our findings reveal that the incongruence between technological and exclusionary values of patent pledges significantly promotes corporate green innovation, while the congruence between the two value forms appears to have no effect. Moreover, the external pressures arising from media reports and government regulations are identified as important contingencies while interpreting the significant impacts of value incongruence on green innovation. Our study tries to unravel how patent pledges foster firms' green innovation, and offers practical suggestions for firms’ strategic actions relating to green innovation.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103636.a: “Ambidexterity” has emerged as the mainstream paradigm in the field of innovation since the study by March (1991). Scholars have conducted extensive research on it, yielding fruitful results. However, despite being an essential dimension of “ambidexterity”, time has largely been viewed as a premise in the past research of ambidextrous innovation, meaning that the temporal mechanism in the process of ambidextrous innovation is still a black box. In this study, we introduce Optimal Matching Analysis (OMA), a technique originating from biology and adapted to social sciences that compares sequence similarity through operations (insertion/deletion/substitution) to map innovation trajectories, as a novel approach to innovation research, with the aim of elucidating on the varied sequence modes of ambidextrous innovation and exploring their innovation performance. Based on the patent and financial data of 538 listed companies in nine strategic emerging industries in China from 1986 to 2021, we reached the following conclusions: (1) The sequence modes of firms’ ambidextrous innovation can be divided into four types based on innovation level and innovation cooperation: exploration focus-cooperation swift mode, exploitation focus-cooperation increase mode, synchronization focus-low cooperation mode, and synchronization focus-cooperation decrease mode. (2) Different sequence modes demonstrate varying innovation performance. Firms in the exploration focus-cooperation swift mode achieve the highest innovation quantity; firms in the exploitation focus-cooperation increase mode attain high quantity but at the expense of quality; firms in the synchronization focus-low cooperation mode have the highest innovation quality; and firms in the synchronization focus-cooperation decrease mode have the lowest innovation performance. Propensity Score Matching (PSM) further validated the robustness of our findings by addressing potential endogeneity concerns. This study pioneers the integration of OMA into the realm of innovation to investigate the sequence mode of ambidextrous innovation. Furthermore, it employs a combination of OMA and regression analysis to examine the influence of diverse ambidextrous innovation sequence modes on firm-level innovation performance. This paper moves beyond the existing hypothesis of “synchronization” or “succession”, opening the black box of time in ambidextrous innovation research, promoting the further application of OMA in ambidextrous innovation, laying a foundation for subsequent sequence research.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103637.a: The rise of industrial digital platforms has accelerated the digital transformation of manufacturing industries. Existing research has examined the structure, value creation, and business models of industrial digital platforms; however, the intrinsic dynamics of platform evolution and the ways in which platform owners empower platform actors remain underexplored. Drawing on dynamic capability theory, this study employs a multi-case approach to explore the evolution and digital empowerment of industrial digital platforms within the steel industry. We identify five micro-foundational dynamic capabilities and three distinct empowerment pathways, revealing that the recursive relationship between platform evolution and empowerment shapes the development and competitiveness of industrial digital platforms. These findings offer a dynamic perspective on the evolutionary processes of industrial digital platforms, demonstrating how platform owners empower actors through informational, material, and financial flows. By highlighting the interplay between platform dynamic capabilities and empowerment mechanisms, this study offers valuable managerial insights for platform stakeholders aiming to navigate and optimize the digital transformation of traditional manufacturing industries.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103638.a: Digital technologies have profoundly transformed healthcare, a phenomenon commonly referred to as Healthcare 4.0. Among these technologies, digital platforms stand out as modular systems that evolve through collaborative and co-creative processes. However, limited attention has been given to how healthcare professionals participate in platform co-creation, how social exchange mechanisms sustain this process, and how tensions emerge from the coexistence of healthcare routines and digital transformation. Drawing on Social Exchange Theory (SET), we examine how trust, commitment, reciprocity, power, and sociotechnical tensions shape internal healthcare platform co-creation. We conducted a qualitative case study in a Brazilian teaching hospital that internalized the development of its primary information system and adopted a co-creative approach in which healthcare professionals assumed Product Owner roles for different platform modules. The empirical investigation combined 25 interviews, participant observation, and document analysis over seven months. The findings show that internal healthcare platform co-creation constitutes a distinct SET configuration in which trust depends on process visibility and responsiveness, reciprocity is associated with professional recognition and shared organizational outcomes, and power is shaped by internal hierarchies and asymmetries in technological expertise. Product Owners emerge as hybrid sociotechnical actors who mediate between healthcare work practices and technical development. Although co-creation enhances smart working by aligning digital solutions with professionals’ needs, it also generates persistent tensions related to technostress, cognitive overload, and competing attention demands between patient care and platform interaction. We argue that these tensions are inherent to healthcare digital transformation and must be continuously managed rather than eliminated.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103639.a: This paper examines how gender and geographic diversity in R&D teams, together with the complexity of national innovation systems (NISs), affect patent quality. While prior research has analyzed these aspects separately, we investigate their interactions and context-dependent effects. Using 32,043 patent families filed between 1991 and 2014 by leading aerospace and defense firms, we estimate several count models to assess the impact of team diversity and NIS complexity on patent quality. Results show that geographic diversity among inventors enhances patent quality, whereas gender diversity does not have a significant independent effect. Contrary to expectations, the interaction of gender and geographic diversity is negative and marginally significant, suggesting coordination challenges may outweigh complementarities. We also find partial evidence that NIS complexity enhances patent quality, though this effect is largely mediated by firm-specific characteristics. Finally, the benefits of geographically diverse collaborations are amplified in complex innovation systems, highlighting the role of robust institutional environments in leveraging spatial diversity in R&D teams.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103640.a: Over the past years profound changes in the public sentiment and policy environment suggest the beginning of a new era with reversal attitudes towards globalization. Deglobalization which is commonly defined as the process of decreasing interdependence among nations has recently become the focus of scholarly attention with particular interest on the deglobalization consequences. A significant question related with deglobalization is how innovation ecosystems adapt in such a new challenging environment. Within this context, the primary objective of this paper is to evaluate the role of deglobalization on the firm's eco-innovation performance directly and indirectly through its moderating effect on eco-innovation spillovers while considering the presence of cosmo-localism. Using a spatially-lagged X model (SLX) for a sample of 63 countries over the period 1990-2023 we shed light on the detrimental effects of deglobalization on eco-innovation performance, emphasizing at the same time the importance of cosmo-localism in terms of alleviating these consequences.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103641.a: How to deliver more value (functionality, sustainability) with limited resources and lower costs (affordability) presents firms with a paradox in developing frugal innovation. This study draws on the resource orchestration theory to investigate the effects of resource orchestration capabilities (i.e., bricolage and exaptation) on frugal innovation. Furthermore, we examined the moderating role of product modularization. We tested our hypotheses using data from 334 manufacturing firms (two managers in each firm) in China. Results show that both bricolage and exaptation foster frugal innovation, which in turn propels firm growth. Product modularization weakens the positive effect of bricolage on frugal innovation but does not strengthen the positive effect of exaptation on frugal innovation. The study contributes to the frugal innovation literature by exploring the mechanisms that drive frugal innovation from the perspective of resource orchestration.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103642.a: The article presents an in-depth analysis of the Entrepreneurship and Innovation Ecosystem (EIE) of Crete, employing the Quintuple Innovation Helix (QIH) framework to explore systemic capabilities and bottlenecks. Drawing on empirical data from 25 regional firms and key innovation actors, the study reveals a science-anchored yet structurally imbalanced ecosystem. While institutions -such as the University of Crete, the Foundation for Research and Technology-Hellas (FORTH) and the Science and Technology Park of Crete (STEP-C)- provide a robust academic base, commercialization pathways, innovation partnerships, and ecosystem coordination remain limited. The analysis uncovers gaps in venture funding, talent specialization, IP strategy, and civil society engagement. By mapping the maturity levels across the five helices—academia, industry, government, civil society, and the environment—the paper identifies strategic asymmetries and proposes two integrated prongs for ecosystem enhancement: structural functionality and firm-level resilience. A six-step roadmap for QIH implementation is outlined to guide regional innovation policy. The findings offer a replicable blueprint for other peripheral ecosystems seeking inclusive, knowledge-driven, and sustainability-aligned innovation growth.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103643.a: The question of how openness affects firm innovation has long been complex and remains insufficiently explored. Drawing on an interdisciplinary knowledge base perspective, this study investigates how openness can be strategically managed to foster firms' key core technology (KCT) innovation. Using panel data from 177 listed firms in China's new energy vehicle (NEV) industry from 2000 to 2023, this study applies a zero-inflated negative binomial regression model to examine how the breadth and depth of openness influence KCT innovation, and how these effects are moderated by firms' interdisciplinary knowledge base. The results indicate that both the breadth and depth of openness exhibit inverted U-shaped relationships with KCT innovation, suggesting that moderate openness is most effective in promoting firms' KCT innovation. Furthermore, interdisciplinary knowledge diversity elevates the peak of the inverted U-shaped relationships for both openness breadth and depth and broadens their effective ranges, while interdisciplinary knowledge balance and disparity respectively attenuate the negative marginal effects of excessive openness breadth and depth. In sum, the study advances understanding of how to strategically manage innovation openness from an interdisciplinary knowledge base perspective to promote firms' KCT innovation, providing both theoretical contributions and practical guidance.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103644.a: While extant research has demonstrated the positive impact of government venture capital (GVC) on innovation within its portfolio firms, the externalities exerted on local peers (defined as unfunded firms operating in the same city and industry sector as the portfolio firms) remain underexplored. To address this research gap, this study analyzes 23,164 GVC investment events in China from 2008 to 2023 and construct city–industry investment shocks to investigate this external effect. We find that GVC entry significantly enhances local peers' innovation performance, generating a distinct innovation ripple effect. Mechanism analysis reveals that this effect operates through two complementary channels: a demonstration-learning effect, whereby local peers learn from GVC-backed benchmarks to reduce innovation uncertainty, and an escape competition effect, which motivates peers to innovate under intensified market pressure. Notably, digital transformation strengthens of both mechanisms by enhancing local peers’ information-processing capacity and resource allocation flexibility. Further analysis indicates that the ripple effect is strongest among local peers with larger firms or those with higher total factor productivity (TFP), in more competitive or high-tech industries, and when GVC targets mature or non-state-owned enterprises (non-SOEs). These findings advance the understanding of GVC from a firm-level financing instrument to an ecosystem-restructuring innovation shock, enrich theories of policy-induced peer effects, and offer practical implications for cluster-level industrial upgrading.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103645.a: This study examines the relationship between national AI capability and labor productivity in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) through the lens of absorptive capacity theory. Rather than focusing on frontier AI innovation, we conceptualize AI capability as a transformation-stage construct emerging from the interaction between AI-embodied external inflows (e.g., AI-related hardware imports) and domestic complementary conditions (e.g., internet penetration, broadband access, electricity access, and financial inclusion). This framing reflects how most LMICs engage with AI—through embodied technology imports combined with enabling structural conditions. Using a panel dataset of 63 LMICs over the period 2005–2019, we construct a novel AI Capability Index via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and estimate its association with labor productivity using two-way fixed effects and system GMM estimators. We complement this analysis with interaction-based specifications that separate AI-related inflows and domestic readiness conditions and examine how their interaction relates to labor productivity. Our results reveal a robust and statistically significant positive association: a one standard deviation increase in AI capability is associated with approximately a 9.20–9.37% increase in labor productivity, depending on index construction (flow-based vs. stock-based). Results remain stable across alternative specifications and sensitivity analyses. These findings indicate that productivity gains in LMICs depend not solely on access to AI-related technologies, but also on the complementary institutional and infrastructural conditions that enable their transformation and diffusion. By operationalizing AI capability as a national-level transformation-stage construct, this study extends absorptive capacity theory beyond the firm level and provides a replicable empirical framework for assessing national AI capability formation and its relationship to labor productivity under data-constrained conditions. In doing so, it contributes to ongoing debates on digital transformation, technological adoption, and capability formation in LMICs.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103646.a: The integration of generative AI into healthcare presents a profound trust dilemma for older adults, a demographic highly sensitive to risk and algorithmic opacity. While existing literature primarily focuses on post-adoption AI interaction design, it largely overlooks the critical pre-adoption phase: how strategic marketing communication persuades vulnerable populations to engage with AI. Addressing this gap, this study investigates how marketing communication orientations: goal-oriented (emphasizing instrumental performance) versus duty-oriented (emphasizing safety and ethical governance) shape older adults’ trust and intention to adopt medical AI. Across three scenario-based experiments, we test a comprehensive behavioral model. Study 1 establishes a critical boundary condition, demonstrating that duty-oriented messaging significantly increases adoption intentions and trustworthiness in abstract, high-uncertainty preventive contexts, whereas this advantage diminishes in concrete, outcome-focused diagnostic and treatment settings. Studies 2 and 3 probe the underlying attributional mechanisms and individual differences by testing corporate motive attributions, AI literacy, and AI risk perception. Our findings reveal that duty-oriented framing enhances values-driven motive attributions, which in turn increase trust and adoption intentions among older adults. Furthermore, the persuasive advantage of duty-oriented communication is amplified for seniors with higher AI literacy. This study contributes to the digital innovation literature by shifting the paradigm from algorithmic interaction design to pre-adoption strategic framing and motive attribution. We provide actionable guidelines for practitioners to embed duty and normative transparency into their marketing to bridge the generative AI adoption gap for older adults.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103647.a: Why do some ventures appear to run on a faster clock than others? We argue that part of the answer lies in the artifacts from which ventures are built. Conceptualizing entrepreneurship as an artifact-mediated design process, we theorize digital artifact properties as temporal operators: they condition the coupling between development and validation and thereby shape the speed, sequencing, concurrency, and granularity of venture creation. Drawing on a longitudinal action design study informed by Action Design Research (ADR) principles, we examine a primary education technology (edtech) venture using time-stamped logs, telemetry, and digital artifacts across four design cycles and a subsequent observation phase. We show how modularity and its generative offspring—reprogrammability, traceability, and distributedness—are actualized through four sociotechnical mechanisms: flexible iteration, concurrent co-creation, decentralized co-creation, and data-driven operations. These mechanisms explain when development and validation overlap, when feedback cycles compress, and when sequential staging reappears. The study advances mechanism-based theorizing in digital entrepreneurship, adds a temporal dimension to entrepreneurship-as-design, and illustrates how ADR principles can support forward-oriented entrepreneurship process research.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103648.a: While Industry 4.0 (I4.0) has led to the proliferation of policy-driven innovation ecosystems aimed at supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in their digital transformation, limited attention has been paid to how managers engage with these environments in practice. This study examines how SMEs’ managers interpret, evaluate, and mobilise external support within I4.0 Regional Innovation Ecosystems (I4.0 RIE). Drawing on 25 semi-structured interviews with managers of industrial SMEs in Belgium, we adopt a sense-making perspective to analyse engagement as an interpretive process. The findings show that managers approach these ecosystems as overlapping support mechanisms, which they evaluate in terms of accessibility and usability and enact through selective, adaptive, and sometimes reversible patterns of access and use. These findings suggest that engagement with I4.0 RIE is not driven by the availability of support alone, but by how managers interpret and position it in relation to their firms’ needs and constraints. By foregrounding these dynamics, the study offers a processual view of how SMEs engage with innovation ecosystems under digital transformation.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103649.a: National protectionism and unilateralism have continued to spread around the world. In particular, the U.S.-China technological decoupling has brought huge economic policy uncertainty to Chinese enterprises and has also profoundly affected their innovation. In this study, we develop a framework for how technological decoupling guides enterprises' knowledge acquisition: internationalization or localization. We use the differences-in-differences (DID) method to study why and how the technological decoupling affects enterprises' knowledge acquisition proxied by patent backward citations. Further, we also explore the heterogeneous effects of the enterprise's proximity to science and state ownership. Our analysis shows that the U.S.-China technological decoupling has reduced Chinese enterprises' knowledge acquisition from the U.S. This result does not exhibit spillover effects to other countries but rather reverse intense effects to own country, and Chinese enterprises affected by technological decoupling have acquired more local knowledge. Heterogeneity analysis results indicate that the effects of technological decoupling leading to a decrease in U.S. knowledge acquisition are more concentrated in enterprises proximity to science and non-state-owned enterprises (SOEs), whereas enterprises with a low degree of proximity and non-SOEs are significantly more impacted in local knowledge acquisition. By redirecting innovation outcomes towards knowledge acquisition, our findings enrich the literature on the impact of technological decoupling on innovation, aiding in the comprehension of changes in enterprise innovation behavior from a technological decoupling perspective.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103650.a: The integration of Industry 4.0 technologies into manufacturing systems has largely emphasized productivity and efficiency, with limited attention to how the inclusion of people with disabilities (PwD) can contribute to and reshape these performance outcomes. Addressing this gap, this study investigates how Industry 4.0 technologies can support workers with sensory and physical disabilities within manufacturing environments. The research employs a qualitative methodology, combining semi-structured interviews with professionals from multinational corporations and specialists in this field as well as analysis of corporate reports to evaluate the effects of technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), collaborative robots (cobots), augmented reality (AR), and exoskeletons in workers inclusion. Findings reveal that these technologies generate upskilling (e.g., AI-enhanced assistive devices for visual impairments), reskilling (e.g., learning how to do quality inspections with multisensory feedback provided by IoT sensors for hearing impairments), and deskilling (e.g., cobot-assisted task simplification for physical disabilities), depending on the disability type and context. The study introduces the concept of “Inclusion 4.0″, positioning Industry 4.0 as a catalyst for equitable workforce participation aligned with the Industry 5.0 human-centric pillar. Practical implications include actionable insights for policymakers and managers to design inclusive industrial systems, while theoretical contributions highlight a socio-technical framework that prioritizes disability-inclusive technological adoption.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103651.a: This study proposes and tests a model that extends the knowledge of business model innovation (BMI)'s drivers, introducing strategic innovation readiness (SIR) as a fundamental mediating mechanism. Drawing on the Resource-Based View theory and the Socioemotional Wealth approach, we test the contingent effect of family firm on this model. Data were obtained from an international European Commission project to assess the relationships proposed. A sample of 417 Small and Medium-sized Enterprises was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. The results indicate that competition intensity positively influences both BMI novelty and BMI scope, with SIR acting as a partial mediator in these relationships. A significant contribution of our multigroup analysis is that the indirect effect of competition intensity on BMI via SIR is stronger in non-family SMEs than in family SMEs. In addition, for non-family firms, SIR fully mediates the competition intensity-BMI scope relationship, whereas for family firms, this mediation is partial. These findings underscore that while both firm types need SIR to innovate, non-family firms exhibit a more pronounced and fully mediated response in broadening their BMI, suggesting distinct strategic pathways driven by inherent firm characteristics. These insights advance the BMI literature, particularly concerning the unique innovation dynamics of family versus non-family firms.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103652.a: Digital platforms have substantially transformed traditional entrepreneurial ecosystems by introducing new business models and opportunities for entrepreneurs to develop complementary products and services. Grounded in entrepreneurial ecosystem studies, digital platform practices, and entrepreneurial behavior theory, we propose a renewed theoretical framework to explain how platform design functions create framed entrepreneurial opportunities, and how entrepreneurs pursue their goals under standardized rules. We apply the fsQCA method to identify successful configurations of platform functions across different types of entrepreneurs based on crowdfunding campaigns from the Indiegogo platform. The findings reveal that novice entrepreneurs tend to adopt a visual strategy, relying on emotional resonance to achieve funding success. Cross-category habitual entrepreneurs are more adept at mobilizing social networks and incentive mechanisms, forming a social strategy. Non-cross-category habitual entrepreneurs, in contrast, depend on well-structured and coherent textual narratives to implement a linguistic strategy. These findings uncover a coupling relationship between platform design functions and entrepreneur types, suggesting that success is not determined by the number of functions used, but by the fit between platform design and entrepreneurs’ capabilities. Our research contributes to both entrepreneurial behavior theory and entrepreneurial ecosystem studies, and offers practical implications for how platforms can tailor differentiated support for various types of entrepreneurs.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103653.a: Ongoing environmental issues are increasingly challenging the manufacturing sector because of its environmental footprint. These issues, including carbon emissions, intensive resource consumption, large-scale waste generation, and environmental pollution, have stimulated demand for environmentally responsible supply chain practices. The implementation of these practices can be realized through the application of advanced technology, such as Industry 4.0. This study examines the role of Industry 4.0 technologies towards sustainable supply chain performance and investigates the mediating role played by circular supply chain practices and visibility. Moreover, the moderating role of strategic alliances and resilient supply chains was also analyzed. Data were collected using time-lagged research from senior managers working in manufacturing companies in China. PLS-SEM was used to analyse 371 questionnaires. The findings suggest that Industry 4.0 enhances supply chain visibility and circular supply chain practices and improves sustainable supply chain performance. Further, results also show that supply chain resilience moderates the association between circular supply chain practices, supply chain visibility, and sustainable supply chain performance. However, the moderating role of strategic alliances was found to be insignificant. These findings reveal that manufacturing organizations can achieve sustainable supply chain performance by integrating Industry 4.0 into their operations. These findings contribute significantly to Industry 4.0 and the circular economy in academic, managerial, and policy debates, resulting in sustainable supply chains. Potentially, the findings serve to drive sustainable supply chains in developing countries to better manage the digital transition of the manufacturing industry.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103654.a: The global aging population, particularly the increasing number of individuals over 65 in Europe, presents both significant challenges and unique opportunities. This demographic shift has sparked the rise of the Silver Economy ( i.e. , a sector focused on the production, consumption and trade of goods and services aimed at improving the lives of the elderly), increasingly driven by technological solutions such as artificial intelligence (AI). Among these technologies, robo-advisors (RAs) hold promise in enhancing the quality of life, autonomy and social inclusion for older adults. However, while the potential of AI to integrate the elderly into society is widely acknowledged, there remain substantial gaps in understanding how best to deploy such technologies. Existing literature reveals critical limitations in methodologies and a lack of comprehensive models to guide the integration of AI into the lives of the elderly. This study addresses these gaps by adopting a constructivist approach and proposing a decision-support system to guide authorities in crafting effective policies and initiatives. The system is developed with input from field experts through participatory methods, specifically the Nominal Group Technique (NGT) and the DEcision MAking Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL), within a neutrosophic framework. By doing so, the study provides a more nuanced understanding of the barriers and opportunities in using RAs for the elderly, offering both theoretical advancements and practical recommendations to improve their integration into the AI-driven future of the Silver Economy.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103655.a: Urban mobility and logistics are being transformed by the adoption of autonomous and uncrewed vehicle systems (UxVs), yet research on user acceptance remains theoretically fragmented and empirically inconsistent. This study systematically reviews empirical research on UxV acceptance, across ground-based autonomous mobility technologies and autonomous logistics and last-mile delivery systems, excluding speculative aerial passenger technologies for which no empirical evidence exists. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), its subsequent extensions (TAM2, TAM3, and TAM for Smart Technologies), as well as the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT and UTAUT2), the review synthesises psychological, social, technological, and contextual determinants of UxV acceptance. Our analysis shows that acceptance arises from the multidimensional interaction of these factors and that no single model fully captures the domain-specific differences between mobility and logistics applications. Contextual influences, such as exogenous shock, organisational dynamics, and institutional and policy frameworks, appear as important moderators that shape, rather than replace, established TAM and UTAUT constructs. The review also identifies significant knowledge gaps, including the influence of socio-demographic variables, the need for technology-specific studies, and the importance of empirical research grounded in real-world trials. Addressing these gaps is essential to advancing theory and informing the effective integration of UxV technologies in complex urban environments.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103656.a: Firms create and manage coopetitive portfolios (i.e., alliance portfolios including competitors) to foster product innovation, as they provide access to various complementary but also compatible resources and knowledge that are essential for innovation. The presence of competitors in coopetitive portfolios can create specific synergies but also conflicts with other partners that could enhance or limit the occurrence of product innovation. To understand under which combinations of partner types in a coopetitive portfolio product innovation can occur, we use a crisp-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (csQCA) on a sample of 921 Dutch firms in the period 2010-2016. We show that alliances with competitors are complementary with customer alliances in promoting the occurrence of product innovation. In addition, our analysis reveals that when ties with universities are present in a coopetitive portfolio, suppliers must be present as well to introduce new products. Finally, we highlight that coopetitive portfolio configurations leading to product innovation vary according to the focal firm's size and industry dynamics.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103657.a: Despite the potential applications of bio-marine technologies, many promising innovations remain confined to the laboratory, missing potential high-value applications and damaging the overall perception of the emerging technology. Prior research has highlighted the positive impact of multi-actor collaborations on technology development, particularly to bridge the gap between the lab and the market. However, we know little about the mechanisms that sustain productive multi-actor collaboration in emerging technology commercialization and why they prove insufficient as actors move from low-to high-value applications. We study the case of an emerging technology – the utilization and application of fucoidan, a bio-marine extract – to explore how collaboration is sustained among actors as they face the increasing complexity of the technology commercialization for high-value applications. By building on patents and publications and analyzing in-depth interviews, we identify three key mechanisms that support effective collaboration: anchoring a shared vision, coordinating across knowledge boundaries, and structuring an operational framework. We show how these mechanisms need to be recalibrated, not simply scaled, when actors transition across problem spaces from low to high-value applications, and why the failure to do so produces a low-value trap for the emerging technology.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103658.a: Whether industrial robot adoption improves firm productivity remains an open question, with mixed evidence echoing the broader productivity paradox associated with information and communication technologies. This paper examines whether firm-level management quality can help resolve this ambiguity. Using novel firm-level data from the China Employer–Employee Survey, which uniquely combines direct measures of robot capital and management practices, we show that robot adoption is associated with significantly higher total factor productivity. This finding is robust to alternative measures of robot use and productivity, as well as to instrumental variable strategies exploiting exogenous robot-policy shocks and firm-level robot exposure. A difference-in-differences design further supports a causal interpretation. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that these productivity gains are strongly moderated by management quality. In particular, monitoring, target-setting, and managerial incentive practices act as key complements, whereas non-manager incentives do not play a significant moderating role. Further analysis shows that the gap in productivity gains from robot adoption between small and large firms narrows at higher levels of management quality, suggesting that managerial capability is a key constraint on small firms’ returns to industrial robots. These findings help reconcile the mixed evidence on robot productivity and underscore the importance of management improvement programs as a complement to automation policy.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103659.a: Drawing on feminist and institutional perspectives, this study analyses whether women are equally likely as men to engage in innovative entrepreneurship and whether the maturity of debt and equity markets strengthens women's participation. We use data from 71,888 early-stage ventures across 101 countries and show that women are as likely as men to engage in innovative entrepreneurship, once crucial individual and country-level factors are controlled for. Further, we demonstrate that both debt and equity market development positively moderate this relationship. These findings reveal that gender gaps in innovative entrepreneurship reflect structural and institutional conditions rather than intrinsic propensities and highlight the role that financial development plays in supporting female innovative entrepreneurship.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103660.a: This paper examines the boundary between human and machine creativity by analysing 593 tasks across 126 occupations in the cultural and creative industries. Theoretically, we propose an evolutionary conceptualisation of creativity, structured around three rule types corresponding to retention (codified), adoption (tacit), and origination (novel) phases. Empirically, using GPT-4, we generate synthetic annotations of the semantic content of task descriptions in the Australian Skills Classification. We derive indicators of cognitive and behavioural rules within tasks and their carriers (human, AI, or hybrid human-AI) to capture creativity, and indicators of AI autonomy feasibility and efficiency potential to capture GenAI exposure scenarios. The agent-rule matching suggests a specialisation of agents in carrying defined, tacit, or novel rules, as well as two mechanisms. The first is the structured novelty effect, whereby AI autonomy feasibility is higher when defined cognitive rules combine with novel rule creation. The second is the tacit knowledge boundary, whereby tacit rules are negatively associated with AI autonomy feasibility. In our interpretation, these mechanisms reflect an efficacy logic (matching the right agent to each rule type) that differs from an efficiency logic (optimising technically feasible gain potentials). Combining both logics, we derive a simulated classification of tasks into three categories. The mixed category, involving hybrid carrier configurations, predominates (86.3%), alongside limited replacement (2.7%) and AI immune (11.0%) categories. We identify two levels of human-AI complementarity. The first lies in rule types within tasks and engages different forms of creativity (combinatorial, exploratory, transformational). The second concerns efficiency potential when performing tasks.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103661.a: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping how innovation is developed, and new product development (NPD) is an important domain at the centre of this shift, given its data-rich, high-uncertainty contexts. In this paper, we focus on the design and training of AI systems in which human expertise is encoded into machine models and the future scope of human and machine agency is determined. Drawing on organizational learning theory, we argue that training strategies defining who provides labels, which data are used, and how feedback is generated and reused, constitute design decisions that differ in how feedback is recursively structured, where knowledge is located, and how deeply expert judgment is codified. We develop and test three strategies, experiential, nudging, and generative, and instantiate them through computational simulations in the domain of geotechnical services for underwater exploration. We further assess the cross-context portability of the most effective strategy by redeploying the trained model in a second NPD setting. Our results show that strategies that recursively incorporate expert feedback across training cycles produce reliable, transferable models, whereas those that decouple human expertise from the training process converge prematurely on narrow solution spaces. These findings suggest that how firms structure the training of AI systems directly shapes model reliability and transferability, and provide a basis for theorizing how organizational routines, competencies, and relational forms of AI agency may develop as AI systems become embedded in NPD processes.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103662.a: Prior research has found that brokers, those who stand between two disconnected parties, may access non-redundant information that is conducive to higher innovation. However, research has also shown that occupying brokering network positions does not systematically translate into higher innovation; in other words, brokers do not always exploit such structural opportunity. To better understand the conditions under which brokers innovate, we adopt a contingency approach and theorize that the relationship between brokerage and individual innovation is contingent on individuals’ perception of their power over alters, an important aspect of individuals’ representation of the situation they are in. Using a social network analysis at a consulting and training organization in The Netherlands, we found support for our theory: employees perceiving higher power over alters achieved higher innovation in brokering network positions than employees in these positions who perceived lower power over alters.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103663.a: As hybrid organizations situated at the nexus of market and state logics, integrator state-owned enterprises (SOEs) face the daunting challenge of navigating competing institutional demands. In the process of CoPS innovation, such tensions coalesce into a persistent trade-off between legitimacy and autonomy. Drawing on an inductive multiple-case study of three large integrator SOEs operating in two representative CoPS domains in China, this study examines how these firms respond to legitimacy–autonomy tensions across different phases of CoPS innovation. We identify two response strategies, namely, aggregate projection and parallel coordination , that address goal conflicts in the goal-setting phase and means conflicts in the resource-allocation phase, respectively. Moreover, we propose a theoretical model illustrating how these mutually constitutive response strategies jointly enable integrator SOEs to secure legitimacy while preserving autonomy in achieving CoPS innovation. These findings deepen the scholars’ understanding of organizational responses to institutional demands, while also contributing to literature on CoPS innovation.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103664.a: Knowledge is a fundamental strategic resource. While extensive research examines how firms expand their knowledge base through acquisitions, less attention has been given to how firms reshape and optimize their knowledge base through divestitures. Drawing on the Knowledge-Based View (KBV), we conceptualize divestitures as a mechanism for knowledge reconfiguration, akin to an innovator’s scalpel, which firms can use to refine their knowledge stock and enhance their capacity for technological recombination. We argue that, on average, divestitures will weaken a firm’s technological performance because they reduce the size of the firm’s knowledge base, disrupt innovation routines, and create organizational uncertainty. However, we propose that when firms divest in a way that enhances their technological, structural, and organizational focus, we argue divestitures can lead to superior technological performance. We test our hypotheses using a sample of 7,138 firm-year observations, covering 919 unique firms, in 4 high-tech industries, that announced 1,794 divestitures and filed 414,128 patent applications over a 15-year period. Our findings confirm that while divestitures generally disrupt innovation, divestitures that create focus leads to more and higher-quality innovation. In doing so, our study provides theoretical and managerial insights into how firms can use divestitures to shape their knowledge base, to sustain long-term technological competitiveness, and drive innovation performance. Importantly, our study also advances the corporate strategy and innovation literature by demonstrating that divestitures can be used as an innovation scalpel, cutting away the excess, to strengthen knowledge cohesion, flow and governance.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103665.a: Combining technology-push and demand-pull instruments into a policy mix has been widely employed by policymakers to stimulate innovation. Prior empirical studies have primarily investigated the impacts of the balance between the two types of instruments within a policy mix on innovation performance at the macro or meso level, with limited attention given to the roles of micro-level policy recipients and the contexts in which policies are implemented. By integrating the motivation-opportunity-ability framework with the resource-based view and institutional theory, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of how the effectiveness of a balanced policy mix in stimulating innovation is contingent upon the internal and external contexts of policy-recipient firms. Our empirical analyses are based on a panel dataset of 77 listed firms in the solar photovoltaic industry of China from 2012 to 2022. We find that the balance between technology-push and demand-pull policy instruments within a policy mix has a positive effect on firm innovation performance. Moreover, this relationship is contingent upon firms’ internal absorptive capacity and regional institutional development, and their relative importance differs between state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and non-state-owned enterprises (non-SOEs). The moderating effect of absorptive capacity is particularly pronounced for non-SOEs, whereas the moderating effect of regional institutional development is primarily salient for SOEs. This study extends the innovation literature on policy mix by shedding light on the innovation effect of policy mix balance at the micro level and its contingencies.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103666.a: Although emerging economies encourage firms to create value through disruptive innovations, less is known about how firms appropriate value from these innovations. Drawing on the profit from innovation (PFI) framework, this study examines how product disruptiveness influences opportunity exploitation and how this relationship is conditioned by appropriability mechanisms and institutional forces. Based on a multi-wave, multi-informant field survey and a scenario-based experiment, we find that product disruptiveness enhances opportunity exploitation by increasing perceived differentiation and perceived attractiveness. This relationship is reinforced by informal appropriability mechanisms and political ties, but diminished by formal appropriability mechanisms and government support. These findings shift attention from value creation to value appropriation in disruptive innovation research and extend the PFI framework by showing that value appropriation from disruptive innovations depends on the fit between appropriability mechanisms, institutional forces, and disruptive innovation trajectories in emerging economies.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103667.a: Crowdsourcing in science is an increasingly popular complementary method of conducting scientific research. However, organizing a crowdsourcing in science initiative is a challenge for scientists, and many such initiatives fail. Nevertheless, the literature on failures of crowdsourcing in science and their causes is still in its infancy, and the results to date are scattered and fragmented. Drawing on a multilevel perspective, we recognize, characterize and offer a structured understanding of the causes of the failure of crowdsourcing in science. We collected data using focus group interviews with 36 scholars representing various scientific fields and disciplines. The results show that the causes of failure are the initiator's insufficient competences, their negative attitude towards crowdsourcing in science, insufficient organisational support, the compulsory nature of crowdsourcing in science, and the crisis of trust in science. In addition, normative pressure and technology connect the interactions within and between levels. On the basis of these findings, we propose a multilevel conceptual framework that structures the causes of the failure of crowdsourcing in science, and takes into account interactions within and between levels. The results and the framework serve as the basis for offering implications for researchers, managerial staff of institutions of higher education and decision-makers. We show how important crowdsourcing in science is, and that careful management of such projects is workable.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103668.a: Trade credit plays a critical role in alleviating firms' short-term financing constraints, yet little is known about how firms adjust their use of trade credit in response to innovation failure. Drawing on the substitution hypothesis between bank credit and trade credit, this study examines how innovation failure, as a firm-level adverse shock, affects firms’ trade credit usage. Using panel data from 296 listed biopharmaceutical firms in China over the period 2007 – 2024, we document a significant U-shaped relationship between innovation failure and trade credit. Specifically, firms’ reliance on trade credit decreases as innovation failure rises from low to moderate levels, reaches its lowest point at moderate levels, and then increases as innovation failure becomes high. We further show that this U-shaped relationship is driven by a substitution mechanism between bank credit and trade credit. In addition, innovation disclosure strengthens the U-shaped relationship by improving information transparency and reducing uncertainty surrounding innovation outcomes. Overall, this study highlights the pivotal role of trade credit in alleviating short-term financing constraints arising from innovation failure from a supply chain finance perspective. It provides new empirical evidence and policy implications for optimizing corporate financing structures through effective supply chain relationship management.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103683.a: A microfoundational account of organizational innovation capability should explain which individual-level attributes distinguish ideators who are better able to generate, select, and elaborate ideas into investment-worthy business concepts. Yet research remains fragmented because prior studies often examine isolated traits and fail to distinguish among key creative ideation outcomes. Drawing on Trait Activation Theory, we conceptualize venture ideation as a staged, trait-relevant context in which cognitive abilities, personality traits, and creative domain experience are differentially expressed across successive stages. We examine this theorizing using a task-based assessment that separates idea quantity , idea originality , and idea quality . Innovation-exposed experts, including R&D experts, managers, and entrepreneurs (n = 208), generated multiple business ideas for a disruptive technology, selected their most promising idea, and refined it into a product or service concept incorporating core elements of a viable business model. Experienced technology-focused venture capitalists evaluated idea quality by indicating whether these concepts merited investment interest. We quantified semantic distinctiveness using multiple large language models as a semantic proxy for selected-idea originality. Divergent thinking predicted idea quantity, but not investor-evaluated idea quality. In contrast, investment-interest judgments were predicted by ideators’ Openness to Experience, creative domain experience, and convergent thinking ability. Overall, our findings show that early-stage venture ideation is not a unitary creative process. Different attributes help ideators generate many ideas and develop selected ideas into investment-worthy business model concepts, advancing a microfoundational account of organizational innovation capability in technology-based venture creation.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103684.a: Sharing-platform small and medium-sized enterprises (SPSMEs) are a critical player in the sharing economy. However, how they innovate their business models in the developing economies setting is still unclear. This is because most research focuses on large sharing-platform firms in developed economies, often treating their business models as relatively static configurations, while explaining their innovation mainly from the firm's internal perspective. Accordingly, we ask: how SPSMEs, that operate in developing economies, adapt and reconfigure their business models over time while responding to challenging external conditions (including weak institutions, regulatory uncertainty, low digital awareness, fragmented provider networks, and limited ecosystem support). Drawing on multiple-case studies comprising seven SPSMEs in Jordan and the UAE, we develop a 3Ts process model (Triggering, Theming and Transforming) which explains how SPSMEs recognise opportunities, define value logics, and reconfigure their digital activity systems over time. We also show that the SPSMEs business ecosystem consists of two networks (the Digital Activity Network and the Digital Business Network), whose actors enable, constrain and redirect the business model innovation process. The study contributes to research on business model innovation (BMI) and the sharing economy literature by showing that BMI in SPSMEs is not a one-off design outcome. Rather, it is an evolving and context-sensitive process shaped by firm-level adaptation and business ecosystem conditions, particularly in developing economies.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103685.a: Digital platform technologies are reshaping traditional linear value chains and are increasingly positioned as primary facilitators of circular economy implementation in electronics manufacturing. This study investigates how leading manufacturers, including Apple, Samsung, Xiaomi, and Dell, use digital platforms to support circular strategies through a comparative multi-case analysis of electronics platform archetypes. The analysis identifies two distinct digital platform archetypes. Premium integrated ecosystems, represented by Apple and Samsung, target higher-value consumer segments and emphasise component integration, lifecycle control, and tightly governed proprietary platforms. These models prioritise repair, refurbishment, and lifecycle extension within highly integrated product–service systems. In contrast, accessible ecosystem orchestrators, such as Xiaomi and Dell, promote broader participation across partners and users, focusing on asset management, service modularity, and affordability for price-sensitive consumers and business clients. The findings highlight how platform design influences circular outcomes, with governance structures, business models, and digital infrastructure needing alignment with market positioning and user needs. Overall, the paper contributes to research on digital platforms and circular business models by clarifying how platform archetypes shape pathways toward more circular electronics systems.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103686.a: Achieving disruptive innovation in new green technology domains (NGTDs) is essential for firms seeking sustainable competitive advantage, addressing climate challenges, and complying with increasingly stringent regulations. Building on research on technological relatedness and entry strategies, this study argues that although entering NGTDs enables firms to pursue technological leadership, the disruptiveness of their subsequent green innovations may be constrained by the technological relatedness between their existing knowledge bases and the new green domains. Moreover, this negative effect is shaped by firms’ NGTD entry patterns. Using patent data from 994 Chinese listed firms from 2008 to 2016 and applying a Heckman selection model, we find that technological relatedness reduces the disruptiveness of green innovation. An irregular entry rhythm exacerbates this negative effect, whereas a faster entry pace mitigates it. These findings advance the literature by integrating the concepts of pace and rhythm of entry into studies of green innovation and by providing evidence from an emerging economy context. The results suggest that firms should balance reliance on existing technological trajectories with exploration of new knowledge bases to enhance disruptive outcomes. This study offers actionable insights for firms and policymakers seeking to accelerate green technological transitions and foster more disruptive, high-impact environmental innovation.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103687.a: This study examines whether and how different types of government support (financial, technological, market) impact the three types of co-creation efforts (product, process, and knowledge co-creation) of SMEs and how these, in turn, impact sustainable innovation outcomes. It also investigates whether digital transformation mediates the positive relationship between the three types of co-creation and sustainable innovation. The conceptual model is tested on an original dataset of 188 SMEs in France, collected in 2025. Findings indicate that product co-creation is positively affected by government technological support, and knowledge co-creation by market support. The mediation effect of digital transformation is confirmed for the relationship between product co-creation and sustainable innovation, while process and knowledge co-creation directly lead to sustainable innovation. The implications of the study for research, policy and practice are discussed.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103692.a: This paper aims to conduct a hybrid study focusing on blockchain-driven healthcare service user empowerment and its applications in e-healthcare concepts, using bibliometric, network, thematic, and content analyses. The study considered 778 published articles from 2016 to 2024 and conducted a network analysis of the 49 most-cited articles in the domain of blockchain-driven healthcare service user empowerment. The results underscore the underlying research areas, which are further clustered into five major principles, namely, data ownership and control, data privacy and security, trust and transparency, incentivization and engagement, and accessibility and equity. The results offer unique insights for theoretical and managerial implications and propose a conceptual framework for future study in this sector.

10.1016/j.technovation.2026.103693.a: Generative artificial intelligence challenges established foundations of innovation legitimacy by decoupling output quality from human effort, intention, and responsibility. When creative outputs no longer provide reliable signals of human agency, legitimacy judgments must be reconstructed through alternative interpretive cues. This study reconceptualizes innovation legitimacy as an inferential process formed under conditions of technological opacity and examines how governance practices shape legitimacy judgments in AI-mediated creativity. Drawing on a survey-based experiment (N = 240), we investigate how configurations of AI involvement, transparency timing, and deepfake-related manipulation cues influence perceived deception, perceived human effort, and perceived authenticity. Legitimacy judgments, operationalized as inferential assessments of deception, effort, and authenticity, are distinguished from their downstream attitudinal and behavioral consequences. The findings show that legitimacy in AI-mediated creativity shifts from output-based evaluation toward governance-dependent sensemaking. Transparency operates as an interpretive mechanism whose effects depend critically on timing, while deepfake cues systematically heighten moral uncertainty and undermine legitimacy. By specifying the microfoundations through which legitimacy breaks down and is partially reconstructed under AI-induced opacity, the study advances innovation theory by reframing legitimacy as a governance-dependent inferential achievement. This reframing differs from existing interpretive and institutional accounts: governance is conceptualized not as a mechanism that generates legitimacy directly through compliance or ceremonial conformity, but as an interpretive infrastructure that shapes the conditions under which audiences can form legitimacy judgments when conventional output-based cues are absent. The findings contribute to debates on AI governance, innovation diffusion, and responsible innovation in contexts characterized by ambiguous agency and uncertainty about algorithmic production processes.
